definition: CAGR is the constant annual rate at which an investment would have grown from its starting value to its ending value over a period, assuming all gains are reinvested. It is a geometric average that smooths out year-to-year volatility and is the standard measure Indian fund fact sheets and advisors use to compare long-horizon performance. Unlike average annual return, CAGR ignores the path taken and reflects only the endpoints.
plainEnglish: The steady yearly rate that would take your starting money to your ending money. If ₹1,00,000 becomes ₹2,00,000 in five years, the CAGR is roughly 14.9%.
example: Purchasing a stock at ₹500 and selling at ₹800 after three years gives a CAGR of about 17%.

definition: XIRR is the annualised internal rate of return computed from a series of cash flows that occur on irregular dates, solving for the discount rate that sets the net present value of all flows to zero. It is the standard method for measuring returns on investments with multiple entries and exits, such as SIPs in mutual funds, and is implemented as the XIRR function in spreadsheet software using a 365-day year convention. Unlike CAGR it reflects the timing and size of each cash flow.
plainEnglish: The true annual return on money you put in bit by bit rather than all at once. Your yearly SIP total may say +12%, but XIRR tells you what your actual invested rupees earned.
example: Twelve monthly SIPs of ₹5,000 followed by a final value of ₹66,000 imply an XIRR in the mid-teens, not simply the total gain divided by twelve months.

definition: The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which the present value of an investment's expected cash inflows equals the present value of its outflows, making the net present value zero. It is used to compare projects or cash-flow streams on a single percentage scale, and it underlies XIRR once cash flows are dated. A project is conventionally considered acceptable when its IRR exceeds the required rate of return or cost of capital.
plainEnglish: The break-even interest rate a project or investment earns on the money tied up in it. If IRR is 15%, the deal is worth doing whenever you could otherwise safely earn less than 15%.

definition: Time-weighted return measures the compound growth of a portfolio by geometrically linking the returns of sub-periods between external cash flows, neutralising the effect of the timing and size of contributions and withdrawals. It is the standard basis on which investment managers are evaluated, because it isolates the manager's decisions from the investor's deposit schedule. Fund NAV-based returns are inherently time-weighted.
plainEnglish: How well a fund manager performed, ignoring when you happened to add or withdraw money. It answers whether the manager grew the pot, not whether your timing of deposits helped or hurt you.

definition: The money-weighted return is the internal rate of return of a portfolio's cash flows, so it weights each period's performance by how much capital was actually invested during that period. It therefore depends on the investor's own timing of contributions and withdrawals, not just the manager's skill. XIRR on mutual fund transactions is the common Indian implementation of this measure.
plainEnglish: Your personal return: it credits or blames you for when you put money in and took it out. Invested heavily just before a rally? Your money-weighted return beats the fund's published return.

definition: The arithmetic mean return is the simple average of a series of periodic returns, computed by summing the returns and dividing by the number of periods. It is an unbiased estimate of the expected one-period return but overstates compound wealth growth whenever returns are volatile. It is commonly quoted in daily or monthly performance statistics.
plainEnglish: The ordinary average of a list of yearly returns. If a fund made +50%, -30%, +20%, the arithmetic mean is about +13.3% a year, though your money actually grew less than that.

definition: The geometric mean return compounds the periodic returns and takes the nth root, giving the single constant per-period rate that would reproduce the ending wealth. It is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean and is the correct measure of realised long-run performance. CAGR is the geometric mean expressed on an annual basis.
plainEnglish: The average that matches what actually happened to your money after gains and losses compound. It is why a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover.

definition: Volatility is the dispersion of an asset's returns, most commonly measured as the standard deviation of periodic returns annualised to a yearly figure. In Indian practice, monthly returns of mutual fund schemes are annualised by multiplying the standard deviation by the square root of twelve, and SEBI's scheme riskometer labels are based on the volatility of scheme returns. Higher volatility means wider swings around the average return.
plainEnglish: How bumpy the ride is. A fund that swings between +30% and −20% is more volatile than one that moves gently around +12%.

definition: Variance is the average of the squared deviations of returns from their mean, measuring how spread out outcomes are around the average. Squaring makes large deviations count disproportionately and gives variance units of percent-squared, so its square root, the standard deviation, is used for interpretation. In portfolio theory, the variance of a portfolio depends on the variances and covariances of its component assets.
plainEnglish: A raw score of how scattered the returns are. It is not intuitive to read by itself, so people usually take its square root to get volatility.

definition: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and expresses the typical distance of returns from their mean in the same units as the returns themselves. It is the most widely quoted single-number measure of risk; for equity mutual funds in India it is published on fact sheets alongside returns. Roughly two-thirds of returns in a normal distribution fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
plainEnglish: The typical amount a return wanders from its average. If a fund averages 12% with a standard deviation of 18%, most years land between about −6% and +30%.

definition: Covariance measures the extent to which two series of returns move together, being the average product of their deviations from their respective means across periods. A positive covariance indicates that the assets tend to move in the same direction and a negative one that they move oppositely; the magnitude depends on units, so correlation is often preferred. Portfolio variance depends on the covariances between every pair of holdings.
plainEnglish: A joint-movement score for two investments. If one tends to rise when the other rises, their covariance is positive; if they zig while the other zags, it is negative.

definition: Correlation is covariance scaled by the two series' standard deviations, yielding a unit-free number between −1 and +1. A value of +1 means returns move in perfect lockstep, −1 means perfect opposition, and 0 means no linear relationship; diversification benefits come from combining assets whose correlation is below one. Correlation estimates are unstable across periods, which is why diversification judged on past correlations can fail in stress markets.
plainEnglish: How tightly two investments move together, on a −1 to +1 scale. Gold and equity often have low correlation, which is why people hold both.

definition: R-squared is the fraction of the variance in one series explained by another in a linear regression, expressed as a proportion from 0 to 1. In performance analysis it measures how much of a fund's return variation is explained by its benchmark or market index, so a low R-squared warns that beta and alpha estimates carry little information. It is the square of the correlation coefficient in a single-factor regression.
plainEnglish: How much of a fund's ups and downs are simply the market's ups and downs. R-squared of 0.9 means the index explains most of the movement; 0.3 means the manager is doing something quite different.

definition: Beta measures the sensitivity of an asset's returns to movements in a market index, computed as the covariance of the asset and the market divided by the variance of the market over the same period. A beta above one implies amplified market swings, a beta below one dampened swings, and a beta near zero implies little market dependence. In Indian equity research, beta is typically estimated against the Nifty 50 or broader indices over rolling windows.
plainEnglish: A number saying how hard your investment swings when the market moves. Beta of 1.3 means the market's 10% fall would typically pull it down about 13%.

definition: Alpha is the excess return of a portfolio over the return predicted by the capital asset pricing model for its level of beta, measuring performance not explained by market exposure. A positive alpha suggests outperformance after adjusting for systematic risk; a negative one suggests underperformance. Because alpha is estimated statistically, its apparent value may not be statistically distinguishable from zero, a point repeatedly made in academic evaluations of fund performance.
plainEnglish: The value the manager added beyond simply riding the market. If the market plus the fund's risk profile would predict +10% and the fund returned +13%, alpha is roughly +3%.

definition: The information ratio divides a portfolio's active return over its benchmark by the volatility of that active return, known as tracking error. It measures how much excess return a manager generates per unit of benchmark-relative risk, making it the standard measure for evaluating actively managed funds against their stated index. Values above roughly 0.5 sustained over long Indian market cycles are generally considered strong, though they are sensitive to the benchmark chosen.
plainEnglish: How much extra return a fund earns for each unit of deviation from its benchmark. High ratio means the fund deviates from the index only when it pays off.

definition: The Sharpe ratio divides the average return earned above the risk-free rate by the standard deviation of returns, measuring reward per unit of total risk. It was introduced by William Sharpe as a reward-to-variability measure for ranking mutual funds, and remains the most widely quoted risk-adjusted performance statistic, including on Indian fund platforms. It penalises upside and downside volatility alike.
plainEnglish: How much return you got for each unit of bumpiness. Two funds both returning 12%: the steadier one has the higher Sharpe ratio.

definition: The Sortino ratio modifies the Sharpe ratio by dividing excess return by downside deviation, the volatility of returns below a target such as zero or the risk-free rate, rather than by total standard deviation. Because investors arguably do not mind upside swings, this makes it a more targeted measure of bad-risk-adjusted performance. It is most informative for strategies with asymmetric return distributions.
plainEnglish: Like the Sharpe ratio, but it only counts the downside wobbles as risk. A fund with big gains but small losses scores better here than under Sharpe.

definition: The Treynor ratio divides excess return over the risk-free rate by beta, measuring return per unit of systematic or market risk. Unlike the Sharpe ratio it assumes the investor holds the portfolio as part of a diversified whole, so only non-diversifiable risk should be compensated. It is most meaningful for well-diversified portfolios and is less useful for concentrated holdings.
plainEnglish: Return per unit of market risk taken. It suits someone who already owns many diversified funds, where the main risk left is the market itself.

definition: The Calmar ratio divides an investment's compounded annual return by the magnitude of its maximum drawdown over the same period, expressing return per unit of worst peak-to-trough pain. It is commonly computed over three-year windows and is popular for evaluating hedge funds and alternative strategies, including in Indian PMS and AIF reporting. It is sensitive to the observation window because there is only one worst drawdown in any sample.
plainEnglish: How much annual return came per unit of the worst dive the investment took. A 15% CAGR with a 30% worst fall gives a Calmar of 0.5.

definition: Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough percentage decline in the value of a portfolio or index over a period, measured from a prior high until a new high is regained. It captures tail pain that standard deviation understates and is routinely quoted for Indian equity indices and funds. The depth matters for the investor experience because recovery from a deep drawdown requires a disproportionately larger gain.
plainEnglish: The biggest fall from a high point to the bottom that followed. A fund that went from ₹100 to ₹60 had a 40% maximum drawdown and needs a 67% gain just to get back.

definition: Drawdown duration is the length of time between a portfolio's peak value and the point at which it first recovers that peak, including both the declining and the recovery phases. It measures the patience required of an investor and complements the severity measure of maximum drawdown. Long durations, even with modest depth, can drive investor exits and therefore matter for behaviour-aware planning.
plainEnglish: How long your money stays below its previous high. A fund can lose only 15% but take four years to climb back to even, which tests anyone's patience.

definition: Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between a portfolio's returns and its benchmark's returns, measuring how closely a fund follows its index. Index funds and ETFs aim for low tracking error, while for active funds a higher number indicates greater benchmark-relative risk and is the denominator of the information ratio. It is distinct from tracking difference, which is the simple return gap over a period.
plainEnglish: How consistently a fund sticks to its benchmark. A pure index fund should have a tiny tracking error; a run-away active fund has a big one.

definition: Semi-deviation is the standard deviation computed using only the returns that fall below a chosen target, such as zero or the risk-free rate, treating upside deviations as zero. It is the denominator of the Sortino ratio and isolates the variability that investors actually dislike. Because it discards half the data it is a noisier estimate than full standard deviation.
plainEnglish: A risk measure that counts only losing surprises. Months where the fund beat its target add nothing to the number.

definition: Skewness measures the asymmetry of a return distribution around its mean. Positive skew means a long right tail of large gains with frequent small losses, negative skew means a long left tail of large losses with frequent small gains, and zero indicates symmetry. Many option-selling strategies exhibit negative skew, earning steadily until rare large losses occur.
plainEnglish: Whether the odd extreme outcome is a windfall or a disaster. Lottery-like distributions are positively skewed; most 'steady income' strategies are negatively skewed.

definition: Kurtosis measures how much of a distribution's variance comes from rare extreme outcomes, known as fat tails. Excess kurtosis above zero, relative to the normal distribution, means returns feature more frequent and larger outliers than a bell curve would predict, a well-documented property of daily Indian market returns. Ignoring kurtosis leads risk models to understate the probability of large moves.
plainEnglish: How much the market specialises in rare, violent moves. Fat tails mean crashes and melt-ups happen more often than a tidy bell curve suggests.

definition: Monte Carlo simulation generates thousands of randomised future return paths for a portfolio, based on assumed means, volatilities and correlations, to estimate the distribution of outcomes such as retirement corpus adequacy or goal-funding probability. It does not predict a single future; it quantifies how wide the range of plausible futures is. Results are only as good as the assumptions fed in and should be stress-tested at lower return and higher inflation assumptions.
plainEnglish: A computer rolls out many possible versions of the future for your investments and counts how often you reach your goal. The output is a probability, not a promise.

definition: The bootstrap estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly drawing samples, with replacement, from the observed data itself. In finance it is used to construct confidence intervals for return estimates, drawdowns and withdrawal-safety without assuming normality, and it preserves the empirical fat-tailed nature of the input data. It cannot create scenarios that never appear in the historical sample, which is its central limitation.
plainEnglish: Reshuffling your actual past returns thousands of times to see what range of outcomes those returns could have produced. It reuses reality rather than assuming a textbook distribution.

definition: Value at Risk is the maximum loss a portfolio is expected to suffer over a specified horizon at a given confidence level, for example a one-day 99% VaR. It is expressed as a rupee amount and is widely used in bank trading-book risk management under Basel-style frameworks and in fund risk reporting. VaR says nothing about how large losses beyond the threshold can be, which is why expected shortfall is used alongside it.
plainEnglish: The loss line you should not cross on a bad day, 99 days out of 100. It deliberately ignores what happens on the one day you do cross it.

definition: Expected shortfall is the average loss in the worst tail beyond the Value at Risk threshold, answering how bad things get when the VaR line is breached. It is a coherent risk measure in the sense that it accounts for tail severity and does not discourage diversification, and Basel standards have shifted trading-book risk measures toward it. In practice it is estimated from historical return tails or via simulation.
plainEnglish: The average of your very worst days. If VaR says the worst 1% of days start at a ₹10,000 loss, expected shortfall says those days average perhaps a ₹18,000 loss.

definition: Regression to the mean is the statistical tendency for extreme observations to be followed by less extreme ones when the extremes partly reflect luck rather than skill. In investing it explains why top-performing funds in one period often deliver ordinary returns next, because high returns involve both skill and favourable noise. It is one of the strongest arguments against chasing recent performance rankings.
plainEnglish: Yesterday's stars tend to come back to ordinary. When something is unbelievably good, part of that goodness was luck, and luck does not repeat on schedule.

definition: Sampling error is the difference between a statistic computed from a sample and the true value in the population, arising purely because a finite sample was observed. It is why a fund's three-year return is an unreliable estimate of its long-run expected return, and why its precision improves with roughly the square root of the number of observations. Confidence intervals around performance estimates shrink slowly as the measurement period lengthens.
plainEnglish: The error you get just because you looked at a limited slice of data. Five years of returns are a small sample, so the 'average' you see could easily be off by a lot.

definition: Survivorship bias is the distortion that arises when analysis includes only funds or companies that still exist, silently excluding those that closed or were wound up. Averages computed on survivors overstate typical outcomes because failures disappear from the record. It affects performance comparisons, index backtests and fund-category averages, and is a standard critique of fund databases.
plainEnglish: Judging a game by the winners who are still at the table. The funds that quietly died are missing from the scoreboard, so average returns look better than they were.

definition: Look-ahead bias occurs when a backtest uses information that would not have been available at the moment the trade decision was supposedly made, such as revised financial data or index constituents known only later. It produces spectacular hypothetical results that cannot be reproduced in live trading. Careful backtests use point-in-time datasets and respect publication lags.
plainEnglish: Testing a strategy with tomorrow's newspaper. It looks brilliant on paper only because the computer secretly knew what happened next.

definition: Overfitting is the fitting of a model so tightly to historical data that it captures noise rather than genuine relationships, causing poor out-of-sample performance. It typically results from testing many strategy variations and keeping whichever worked best in the past, a process known as data snooping. Out-of-sample and cross-validated testing, alongside a preference for simple models, are the standard defences.
plainEnglish: Torturing the data until it confesses. A rule that 'worked' in every past year by design usually breaks the moment real money is on it.

definition: A time series is stationary when its statistical properties, such as mean, variance and autocorrelation, remain constant over time. Most forecasting and regression techniques assume stationarity, but many financial series, such as prices and dividend levels, are non-stationary while their returns or changes may be approximately stationary. Non-stationary variables can produce spurious regressions with high apparent explanatory power.
plainEnglish: A series whose habits do not change over the decades you study it. Price levels wander off forever, but day-to-day percentage changes tend to keep similar habits.

definition: Autocorrelation is the correlation of a time series with its own lagged values, measuring the degree to which today's value depends on yesterday's. Positive autocorrelation in returns implies momentum and negative implies mean reversion; in volatility, autocorrelation is strongly positive, which underpins volatility clustering and GARCH-style models. Autocorrelated residuals also violate standard regression assumptions and inflate the apparent significance of estimates.
plainEnglish: Whether today's move remembers yesterday's. Momentum stocks show positive autocorrelation; jumpy, mean-reverting prices show negative.

definition: A quantile is a cut point dividing a probability distribution into intervals with equal probabilities, such as quartiles, quintiles or percentiles. Quantiles are used to describe distributions and to estimate tail measures: the 5% quantile of a return distribution is the threshold below which the worst 5% of outcomes fall. In portfolio construction they underpin quantile-based risk budgeting and scenario analysis.
plainEnglish: A dividing line that slices outcomes by how likely they are. The 10th-percentile outcome is the one that is only better than the worst one-tenth of possibilities.

definition: A percentile is the value below which a given percentage of observations fall, so the 75th percentile of a return series is the level exceeded by only a quarter of observations. Fund platforms commonly show a scheme's percentile rank within its category for rolling periods. Percentile comparisons depend on the peer set and period chosen, so they should not be read as intrinsic quality measures.
plainEnglish: Your position in the queue: the 90th percentile means you scored better than 90 out of 100 peers. It says nothing about whether the whole group did well.

definition: A discount factor is the multiplier that converts a future cash flow into its present value for a given rate and time, equal to one divided by one plus the rate raised to the number of periods. A sequence of discount factors, one per period, defines the discounting used in net present value calculations and in bond pricing, where the factors are drawn from the yield curve. Discount factors at different horizons are the primitive objects from which present values are constructed.
plainEnglish: The shrinking factor applied to money arriving later. At 10%, ₹100 a year from now is worth about ₹91 today, so its discount factor is about 0.91.

definition: Net present value is the sum of the present values of all cash inflows and outflows of an investment, discounted at a rate that reflects its opportunity cost of capital. A positive NPV indicates that the investment adds value at that discount rate, while a negative NPV indicates it destroys value; NPV and IRR are the standard pair of appraisal tools. Unlike IRR, NPV is expressed in rupees and does not suffer from multiple-solution problems when cash flows change sign more than once.
plainEnglish: What all the future money the investment will bring is worth today, minus what you put in. A positive number means the deal beats your required rate.

definition: The effective annual rate converts a nominal rate compounded more than once a year into the equivalent annual rate that accounts for compounding within the year. It allows fair comparison of products quoted with different compounding frequencies, such as monthly-compounded fixed deposits. The gap between nominal and effective rates widens with both the stated rate and the compounding frequency.
plainEnglish: What a quoted interest rate actually earns over a year once the within-year compounding is counted. A 12% rate compounded monthly is really about 12.7% a year.

definition: A nominal rate is the stated rate before adjusting for inflation, while a real rate is the nominal rate adjusted for the change in purchasing power, approximately the nominal rate minus inflation. Real rates govern whether savings actually grow in what they can buy; Indian fixed deposits have at times delivered negative real returns when inflation exceeded deposit rates. Investment decisions about long-term goals should be framed in real terms.
plainEnglish: Nominal is the number on the bank board; real is that number minus inflation. An 8% deposit with 6% inflation is really growing your buying power at about 2%.

definition: The Fisher equation states the exact relationship between nominal rates, real rates and inflation: one plus the nominal rate equals one plus the real rate times one plus expected inflation. It clarifies that nominal interest rates embed compensation for expected inflation, which is why lenders demand higher rates when inflation expectations rise. The approximation real equals nominal minus inflation is close only when rates and inflation are low.
plainEnglish: The precise arithmetic linking the quoted rate, the true growth in buying power, and inflation. It is the formula behind the popular short-cut of subtracting inflation from the rate.

definition: The rule of 72 is a mental-maths approximation stating that the number of years required to double an investment at a constant compound rate is roughly 72 divided by the percentage rate. It is reasonably accurate for rates between about 4% and 15% and is widely used to give intuitive meaning to return assumptions. The exact doubling time comes from logarithms and differs slightly from the approximation.
plainEnglish: Quick doubling maths: at 12% a year money doubles in about six years (72 divided by 12); at 6% it takes about twelve.

definition: Yield to maturity is the single discount rate that equates the present value of all remaining coupon payments and the redemption amount of a bond to its current price, assuming the bond is held to maturity and all coupons are reinvested at that same rate. It is the standard measure of a bond's expected annualised return and is quoted on Indian corporate bond and G-sec screens. Its key limitation is the reinvestment assumption, which rarely holds exactly.
plainEnglish: The total annual return you would earn on a bond if you kept it to the end and could reinvest every interest cheque at the same rate. It is the bond world's equivalent of an interest rate on your purchase price.
example: A bond paying ₹70 a year with three years left and a ₹1,000 face value, bought at ₹980, has a YTM slightly above its 7.14% current yield.

definition: Yield to call is the return computed to the earliest date on which the issuer may redeem a callable bond at the specified call price, rather than to final maturity. It is the relevant yield when the bond is trading near or above its call price and redemption is plausible. Comparing YTM and YTC reveals how much of a callable bond's quoted return depends on the issuer's redemption decision.
plainEnglish: The return if the borrower pays the bond back early, as the fine print allows. If that early payoff is likely, the lower of YTM and YTC is the honest number.

definition: Current yield is a bond's annual coupon amount divided by its current market price, ignoring any gain or loss on redemption and the time value of money. It is a quick income measure but diverges from YTM when the bond trades away from par. Market commentary often quotes current yield while the more complete YTM governs the actual economics.
plainEnglish: The interest you get this year as a percentage of what the bond costs today. Simple to compute, but it ignores whether you eventually get your full money back.

definition: The coupon rate is the annual interest rate stated on a bond, applied to its face value to determine each periodic interest payment. It is fixed at issuance for plain vanilla bonds, may be floating or step-up for structured varieties, and is distinct from the yield an investor actually earns, which depends on purchase price. Interest on most bonds is taxable at the investor's slab rate unless a specific exemption applies.
plainEnglish: The advertised interest rate on a bond, counted on its face value. A 7% coupon on a ₹1,000 bond pays ₹70 a year, whatever you paid for it.

definition: The clean price of a bond is its quoted price excluding accrued interest since the last coupon date, which is the convention on exchange and dealer screens. The buyer pays the dirty price, equal to the clean price plus accrued interest, at settlement. Indian government securities and corporate bonds are typically quoted on a clean-price basis.
plainEnglish: The sticker price of the bond, not counting the interest that has quietly piled up since the last payout.

definition: The dirty price is the clean price plus accrued interest and is the actual amount the buyer pays the seller at settlement. It reflects the seller's entitlement to interest earned up to the sale date, ensuring each holder receives only the compensation for the period the bond was held. Bond pricing formulas based on discounted cash flows produce the dirty price directly.
plainEnglish: What actually leaves your account: the bond's quoted price plus the interest it has earned since the last payout, paid to the seller.

definition: Accrued interest is the coupon interest that has accumulated on a bond since its last payment date, calculated on a day-count convention, and it changes hands when the bond is traded. It ensures the seller is paid for the interest earned during the holding period and the buyer receives the full coupon on the next payment date. Day-count conventions differ between instruments and markets.
plainEnglish: The interest the bond has earned since the last interest cheque that has not been paid out yet. Whoever sells the bond gets their share of it from the buyer.

definition: Face value is the principal amount a bond or debenture promises to repay at maturity and the amount on which the coupon is calculated. In India corporate bonds typically carry a face value of ₹1,000 or ₹10 lakh depending on the market segment, while many equity shares carry a nominal face value that is unrelated to market price. A bond trades at a premium or discount when its price differs from face value.
plainEnglish: The original amount the investment promises to give back, and the base on which interest is counted. A ₹1,000 bond returns ₹1,000 at the end, though you may buy it for more or less.

definition: Redemption value is the amount the issuer pays the bondholder at maturity, which may equal face value for a plain bond or exceed it for a premium-redemption structure, and may be defined by a redemption formula for amortising securities. The difference between redemption value and purchase price generates capital gain or loss, with tax treatment depending on the instrument and holding period. Redemption terms are specified in the offer document or trust deed.
plainEnglish: What you actually get back at the end. Usually the face value, but some bonds promise a little extra as a bonus for lending for so long.

definition: Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time, in years, until a bond's cash flows are received, expressed in units of time. A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its time to maturity, while coupon-paying bonds have shorter durations because coupons arrive earlier. It is the foundation from which modified duration and immunisation strategies are derived.
plainEnglish: The bond's effective waiting time — the average moment its cash flows reach you, weighted by the money involved. Higher coupons mean you get paid sooner on average.

definition: Modified duration divides Macaulay duration by one plus the yield per compounding period and approximates the percentage price change of a bond for a one-percentage-point change in yield, with the sign reversed. It is the primary interest-rate risk measure quoted on Indian bond funds and debt portfolios, where a duration of 4 means a 1% yield rise costs roughly 4% of value. The approximation becomes poorer for large yield changes unless convexity is also considered.
plainEnglish: A sensitivity dial for bonds: duration 4 means prices move about 4% for every 1% move in interest rates, in the opposite direction.
example: A debt fund with modified duration 3.5 would lose roughly 3.5% if yields rose by one percentage point, before convexity effects.

definition: Effective duration measures price sensitivity to a parallel shift in the benchmark yield curve using the full valuation of the bond at slightly higher and lower yields, rather than the closed-form modified duration formula. It is the appropriate measure for bonds with embedded options, such as callable or puttable securities, where expected cash flows change when yields move. The calculation requires a model of how the embedded option behaves.
plainEnglish: Like ordinary duration, but it works for bonds with tricky fine print (like early-repayment clauses) because the computer re-prices each scenario.

definition: Key rate duration measures a bond portfolio's sensitivity to a change in a single point on the yield curve, holding other tenors constant, so a portfolio's exposure can be decomposed across maturities. It is used for curve-risk management: a portfolio may be duration-neutral overall yet still lose money if the curve steepens. Multiple key rate durations at standard tenors together describe the full curve exposure.
plainEnglish: Duration checked point by point along the maturity ladder. A fund can be safe against a general rate move yet still hurt if short-term rates rise while long-term rates fall.

definition: Convexity measures the curvature of a bond's price-yield relationship, capturing the second-order effect that duration alone misses. Positive convexity means gains from falling yields exceed losses from equal rises, making convex bonds more valuable, all else equal; the effect matters most for large yield moves and long-duration bonds. Duration plus a convexity adjustment provides a substantially better approximation of price change.
plainEnglish: The bonus curvature of bonds: prices rise a bit more when rates fall than they drop when rates rise by the same amount. It is a quiet source of advantage.

fullName: Dollar Value of a Basis Point
definition: DV01, also called PV01, is the change in the value of a bond or portfolio for a one-basis-point, that is 0.01 percentage point, parallel move in yields, expressed in currency. It converts percentage duration sensitivity into a rupee amount, which traders use to size hedges and position limits. For example, hedging a portfolio to zero DV01 neutralises small parallel rate moves.
plainEnglish: How many rupees a bond would win or lose if interest rates wiggle by a tiny one hundredth of a percent. Traders use it to measure risk in money, not percentages.

definition: A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 100 basis points equal 1%. It is the standard unit for quoting changes in interest rates, credit spreads and fund expense ratios, because small differences matter in those contexts. RBI policy rate changes are conventionally expressed in basis points.
plainEnglish: A fintech-sized unit of interest: 25 basis points is a quarter of one percent. It exists so people can say small differences precisely.

definition: The credit spread is the difference between the yield on a bond and the yield on a benchmark of comparable maturity, typically a government security, and represents compensation for credit risk and liquidity. Spreads widen when default concerns rise or risk appetite falls and compress in benign markets. In India, corporate bond spreads over the corresponding G-sec or the Mumbai Interbank rates are watched as a barometer of credit conditions.
plainEnglish: The extra interest a borrower must pay over the government's rate because it is riskier. The shakier the borrower, the wider the spread.

definition: The G-spread is a bond's yield minus the yield of a government security with comparable maturity, expressed in basis points and measured as a simple vertical difference between the two yields. It is the simplest credit spread measure and is widely quoted for Indian corporate bonds because the G-sec curve is the reference risk-free curve. It can be distorted when a true same-maturity government bond is unavailable.
plainEnglish: The bond's rate minus the government's rate for the same length. It shows in one number how much extra a company must pay to borrow.

definition: The Z-spread, or zero-volatility spread, is the constant spread that must be added to each point on the benchmark spot yield curve so that discounting the bond's cash flows reproduces its observed price. Unlike the G-spread it recognises that a bond's cash flows arrive at multiple maturities, so it is more precise for longer-dated bonds. It assumes the bond will not be called and is expressed in basis points.
plainEnglish: The extra yield demanded of a bond, calculated properly across all its future payments, not just compared to one point on the government curve.

definition: The option-adjusted spread is the constant spread over the benchmark curve that, when applied to a modelled set of option-adjusted cash flows, reconciles a bond's price with its value. It isolates the compensation for credit and liquidity risk from the value of embedded options such as call or put features. A bond with a call option held by the issuer typically has a lower OAS than its Z-spread suggests, because the option benefits the issuer, not the investor.
plainEnglish: The honest extra yield on a bond after stripping out the value of its fine-print clauses, so you can compare it fairly with simpler bonds.

definition: Probability of default is the likelihood that a borrower fails to meet its debt obligations within a specified horizon, usually one year, as defined in credit-risk frameworks used by banks and in Basel standards. It can be estimated from historical default rates by rating category, market-implied from bond spreads, or modelled statistically from borrower characteristics. PD is one of the three inputs, with loss given default and exposure at default, to expected credit loss.
plainEnglish: The odds that a borrower simply stops paying. Lenders estimate it the way insurers estimate accident rates, from the past behaviour of similar borrowers.

definition: Loss given default is the proportion of an exposure that a lender expects to lose if a borrower defaults, equal to one minus the recovery rate, and it reflects collateral, seniority and workout efficiency. Secured loans have lower LGD than unsecured ones because collateral can be liquidated, though Indian recovery timelines under insolvency proceedings affect realised figures. LGD is a standard input to expected credit loss alongside probability of default and exposure at default.
plainEnglish: How much of the loan you lose when the borrower defaults, after selling any security and chasing the money. A loan secured on gold loses little; a credit-card default loses most of it.

definition: The recovery rate is the proportion of the outstanding exposure that is eventually recovered after a default, through collateral sale, settlement or the insolvency process. India's corporate insolvency framework has produced a wide range of realised recovery rates across sectors, and retail recoveries depend heavily on collections infrastructure. Recovery rates are inversely related to loss given default.
plainEnglish: The slice of your money you actually manage to get back after a borrower flops. It might come from selling their collateral or from a long legal process.

definition: Expected credit loss is the statistical average loss on a loan or portfolio, computed as probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default for each exposure and aggregated. It is the basis of provisioning under expected-loss accounting frameworks and is distinct from actual realised losses in any particular year. Indian banks move between regulatory provisioning norms and expected-loss approaches in line with RBI guidance.
plainEnglish: The average loss the lender budgets for in advance, allowing for the borrowers who will fail. It is like a shopkeeper budgeting for a predictable amount of breakage.
example: A ₹1,00,000 unsecured loan with 4% annual default probability and 70% loss given default carries an expected annual credit loss of about ₹2,800.

definition: Exposure at default is the total outstanding amount a lender expects to be owed at the moment a borrower defaults, including drawn balances and a modelled estimate of undrawn credit lines that will be drawn before default. For term loans it approximates the outstanding principal; for revolving credit such as credit cards or overdrafts it can exceed the current balance. It is the third input, with probability and loss given default, of expected credit loss.
plainEnglish: The size of the bill at the moment the borrower stops paying. For a loan it is what is still owed; for a credit card it can include last-minute spending before things go bad.

definition: A credit rating is an independent agency's forward-looking opinion on a borrower's or debt instrument's ability to meet its obligations, expressed on an alphanumeric scale from the highest safety grades to default. Indian ratings are assigned by agencies registered with SEBI, such as CRISIL, ICRA and CARE, using scales like AAA, AA and A with plus and minus modifiers, and BBB and below for lower safety. Ratings reduce information asymmetry but are opinions subject to revision, not guarantees.
plainEnglish: A report card for borrowers, from AAA (very safe) downwards. It is an opinion about the chance of being paid, not a promise, and it can be downgraded.

definition: Rating migration is the movement of an issuer or instrument from one credit rating category to another over time, captured in transition matrices that show the historical frequency of upgrades, downgrades and defaults by starting grade. Rating migration matters for bond investors because a downgrade widens the credit spread and lowers the price of a held bond even before any default. Sudden multi-notch downgrades of Indian issuers have historically triggered sharp repricing events in credit markets.
plainEnglish: A borrower's report card changing — usually for the worse, when business falters. Even the threat of a downgrade makes the bonds cheaper to sell, and the holder loses.

definition: Credit enhancement is any structural feature that improves the credit quality of a debt security, such as over-collateralisation, subordination of junior tranches, cash reserves or a guarantee from a stronger entity. It is common in Indian securitisation transactions and in bond issues by entities with weaker standalone profiles. Enhancement shifts risk between parties and its benefit depends on the creditworthiness of the party providing it.
plainEnglish: Extra safety padding built into a security: a cushion of spare collateral, a guarantee from a stronger company, or a junior slice that absorbs losses first.

definition: A covenant is a contractual promise by a borrower in a loan or bond agreement, typically either an affirmative undertaking such as maintaining insurance or a negative restriction such as limits on additional borrowing, dividends or asset sales. Financial-maintenance covenants set ratios the borrower must keep, and their breach can trigger acceleration or default. Indian debenture trust deeds and facility agreements set out covenant packages negotiated between borrower and lenders.
plainEnglish: House rules the borrower accepts: for example, not taking on too much extra debt or not selling key assets. Breaking them lets lenders demand repayment early.

definition: Collateral is an asset pledged to a lender that can be sold to recover a debt if the borrower defaults, reducing the lender's loss given default and often the interest rate demanded. Common Indian examples include property mortgages, gold, shares pledged in demat form and hypothecation of business assets. Perfection of security through registration with the relevant registry, such as company-charge filings, determines enforceability.
plainEnglish: Something valuable the borrower hands over as backup. If the loan goes unpaid, the lender can sell it to get their money back.

definition: A debenture is a debt instrument issued by a company, generally bearing a stated interest rate, with repayment of principal at maturity and usually secured by a charge on company assets in the Indian market. Every public issue of debentures above the regulatory size limit must appoint a debenture trustee to protect holder interests, and the terms are recorded in a trust deed. The distinction from a bond is largely convention: bonds are typically used for government and large institutional issuance, while debentures often describe corporate secured debt in Indian usage.
plainEnglish: A company borrowing money from investors in slices, promising interest and repayment, often with company assets pledged behind it.

definition: A non-convertible debenture is a corporate debt instrument that, unlike a convertible debenture, cannot be converted into equity shares and is redeemed in cash at maturity. NCDs may be secured or unsecured, listed on exchanges, and are issued to the public or privately, with public issues requiring a prospectus and a credit rating. Retail investors commonly purchase listed NCDs on stock exchanges or apply to public issues, and interest is taxed at the investor's slab rate.
plainEnglish: A company loan that pays you interest and returns your money at the end but can never turn into shares. Some pay monthly or yearly interest; you check the rating before buying.

definition: A market-linked debenture is an unsecured debt instrument whose final payoff is linked to the performance of an underlying market index or security, subject to a minimum guaranteed amount, thereby combining a bond floor with equity participation. In India MLDs are typically issued as unlisted, privately placed instruments with face values far beyond retail scale, and their returns are taxed according to the special regime applicable to such instruments, distinct from ordinary interest income. SEBI regulates the qualified investor base and issuance framework for these products.
plainEnglish: A bond that keeps a safety net but rolls part of its payout with the stock market, like a fixed deposit with a share-market bonus attached.

definition: A zero-coupon bond pays no periodic interest and is issued at a discount to face value, with the entire return arising from the difference between purchase price and redemption proceeds. Because there are no intermediate coupons, its Macaulay duration equals its time to maturity, making it highly sensitive to interest rate changes. In India, zero-coupon instruments include certain Treasury Bills, and for tax purposes the accretion is generally treated as interest income unless specific rules provide otherwise.
plainEnglish: A bond that pays no interest cheques at all. You buy it cheap, for example at ₹75, and get ₹100 back on maturity, and the ₹25 is your entire earning.

definition: A deep discount bond is issued at a substantial discount to face value and pays either a low coupon or no coupon, so a large part of the investor's return comes as capital accretion over a long maturity. The category spans zero-coupon bonds and bonds with very low coupons relative to their issue spread over government yields. Its long effective duration makes it especially sensitive to changing interest rates.
plainEnglish: A bond sold for far less than its final payout, with most of the gain stored up for the end rather than paid along the way.

definition: A floating rate note pays interest that resets periodically at a spread over a reference rate, such as the Treasury Bill yield or a market benchmark, insulating the holder partly from interest rate risk within each reset period. Because the coupon adapts to prevailing rates, FRN prices are less sensitive to parallel rate changes than fixed-coupon bonds, though they carry reset timing and basis risk. Indian public-sector entities and banks issue FRNs in domestic and offshore markets.
plainEnglish: A bond whose interest rate is re-set from time to time, so it never gets stuck paying an out-of-date rate. In exchange, your income can also fall when rates fall.

definition: A perpetual bond has no fixed maturity date and pays interest indefinitely, with principal repayment occurring only at the issuer's option or upon winding up, subject to the terms of the instrument. Perpetual debt is typically subordinated and counted as capital by issuers such as banks, with call options exercisable only with regulatory approval in India. Its duration is finite mathematically because distant cash flows have small present values, but it is long and highly rate-sensitive.
plainEnglish: A bond that never officially ends and keeps paying interest year after year. You get your original money back only if the issuer chooses, so these are for investors who read the fine print.

definition: Additional Tier 1 bonds are perpetual, deeply subordinated instruments issued by banks to raise capital that qualifies as regulatory Tier 1 equity capital under Basel norms adopted by the RBI. They typically carry high coupons with call options after specified periods, absorb losses by writing down or converting to equity when regulatory trigger conditions on the issuer's capital are breached, and suspend distributions under defined circumstances. Because of the write-down feature, the risk of an AT1 instrument is quite different from the credit risk of the same bank's deposits.
plainEnglish: High-interest bank bonds that officially count as safety cushion for the bank, paid for with real risk: in extreme trouble, they can be written off or turned into shares.

definition: Subordinated debt ranks below deposits and senior debt in the repayment queue if the issuer is wound up, receiving payment only after senior claims are settled. In Indian banking it counts towards regulatory capital if it meets conditions including minimum maturity, and in corporate structures it is used in mezzanine financing layers. Investors demand higher yields for the higher expected loss given default.
plainEnglish: A loan that waits at the back of the queue when a company fails. You are paid only after everyone more senior gets theirs, so you are paid more interest for standing last.

definition: Securitisation is the pooling of homogeneous financial assets, such as mortgages or vehicle loans, into a special purpose entity that issues marketable securities backed by the pool's cash flows. Investors receive payments from the underlying receivables rather than from the originator's balance sheet, and credit enhancement structures allocate losses across tranches of varying seniority. RBI guidelines frame securitisation of standard assets by banks and NBFCs in India, and SEBI regulates the issuance of security receipts on the capital markets side.
plainEnglish: Many small loans are packed together into one big packet, and investors buy shares of the packet's monthly repayments. It lets lenders hand off loan risk and gives investors a new income product.

definition: A pass-through certificate is a security that entitles the holder to a defined share of the principal and interest collections from an underlying pool of receivables, with cash passing through from borrowers to certificate holders. PTCs are issued under securitisation transactions regulated by RBI directions for banks and NBFCs, and their senior or subordinated status determines loss allocation. The payouts are typically monthly but are not a guaranteed fixed return, because they depend on the performance of the pool.
plainEnglish: A certificate proving you own a slice of many loans bundled together. Money that borrowers repay flows through to you, so your monthly income depends on them keeping up.

definition: A repo is a short-term collateralised borrowing arrangement in which one party sells securities, usually government securities, to another with a simultaneous agreement to repurchase them at a slightly higher price on a later date. The price difference is the repo interest rate, and the transaction is effectively a secured loan against the securities, in the Indian market governed by RBI directions and used by banks for liquidity management. The repo rate is also the RBI's principal policy signal.
plainEnglish: A short-term pawn deal between financial institutions: hand over government bonds as security, take cash today, buy the bonds back soon at a small agreed markup.

definition: A reverse repo is the mirror image of a repo: a party lends cash against securities and earns the reverse repo rate, agreeing to sell the securities back later. In central banking, the RBI's reverse repo operations absorb liquidity from the banking system when the stance requires it. For a bank, a reverse repo with the RBI is a nearly riskless short-term placement.
plainEnglish: The same pawn deal viewed from the other side: you have cash to spare and temporarily hold someone's bonds as security while earning a small interest.

definition: A Treasury Bill is a short-dated government debt instrument, issued at a discount to face value by the Government of India and redeemed at par at maturity, with tenors typically spanning a few weeks to a year. Because they are sovereign obligations and have negligible credit risk, their yields anchor the very short end of the Indian risk-free curve, and resident retail investors can bid for them through RBI Retail Direct. The implicit yield reflects the discount and the holding period.
plainEnglish: A very short loan to the government: you pay less than ₹100 today and get ₹100 in ninety days or so; the gap is your earning.

definition: State Development Loans are dated securities issued by individual state governments through RBI auctions to fund their capital expenditure, carrying coupon interest and a fixed maturity. They are eligible for SLR purposes like central government securities but typically trade at a small spread over comparable G-secs because of narrower secondary-market liquidity. Retail investors can access SDLs through RBI Retail Direct.
plainEnglish: A state government borrowing money by selling bonds, almost as safe as central government bonds but usually paying a slightly higher interest rate because they trade less actively.

definition: A Government Security is a dated debt obligation of the Central Government of India, issued through RBI auctions and carrying periodic coupon payments and a maturity date at which principal is repaid. Because the sovereign can raise taxes and borrow in its own currency, G-secs are treated as the domestic risk-free asset and their yields form the benchmark curve for pricing all rupee debt. Retail investors can hold G-secs directly via RBI Retail Direct.
plainEnglish: A loan to the Indian government: it pays you fixed interest half-yearly and returns your money on a set future date. It is the safest rupee investment there is.

definition: Gilt is the market term for government securities, particularly dated obligations of the Government of India, and by extension for gilt funds that invest predominantly in such securities. Gilt prices are driven by interest rate expectations rather than credit risk, so gilts and gilt funds carry interest rate risk even though default risk is negligible. The term historically referred to British government bonds and is now used generically for high-grade sovereign debt.
plainEnglish: An old-fashioned name for government bonds. They never default, but their prices still dance as interest rates move.

definition: The yield curve plots yields of bonds of identical credit quality against their maturities, showing the term structure of interest rates at a point in time. In India it is typically the par or zero-coupon curve of government securities, built from auction and secondary-market data by agencies including the Clearing Corporation and the RBI. Expectations of future policy rates, inflation, and term and liquidity premia determine its shape.
plainEnglish: A line showing what the government pays for loans of different lengths, from a few weeks to thirty years. From it, banks read the future — interest rates, inflation, the mood of the market.

definition: An inverted yield curve occurs when short-term bond yields exceed long-term yields, a pattern that signals expectations of sharply falling future interest rates, often associated with an approaching economic slowdown. It violates the usual upward slope caused by term premia and is closely watched because inversions in major bond markets have preceded recessions before. For investors, an inverted curve rewards staying short and penalises locking into long maturities at low yields.
plainEnglish: An upside-down interest-rate ladder: the bank pays more for one-year money than for ten-year money, usually a warning sign about the economy ahead.

definition: The term premium is the extra expected return that investors demand for holding a long-dated bond instead of rolling over a sequence of short-dated instruments, arising from uncertainty about future rates and inflation over long horizons. It is the main reason the yield curve normally slopes upward even when short-rate expectations are flat. When the term premium compresses or turns negative, long bonds become unattractive relative to their risk.
plainEnglish: The bonus for committing your money for a long time rather than keeping it available. Lenders want something extra in exchange for waiting longer with no escape.

definition: The liquidity premium is the extra yield investors require to hold an instrument they cannot quickly sell at a fair price without moving the market. It is a component of credit spreads and of the spread between off-the-run and on-the-run government securities, and it widens sharply in stressed markets. Less-traded Indian corporate bonds and SDLs typically carry a liquidity premium over benchmark securities of comparable credit quality.
plainEnglish: Payment you demand for the risk of being stuck: if hardly anyone trades the bond, you want extra interest for the trouble of selling it when you need cash.

definition: Reinvestment risk is the risk that coupon payments or maturing principal can only be reinvested at a lower rate than the yield originally earned, reducing the realised compound return relative to the promised yield to maturity. It is highest for high-coupon, long-dated bonds in a falling-rate environment, and it is partly offset by price gains on such bonds. Zero-coupon bonds eliminate reinvestment risk because there are no interim cash flows.
plainEnglish: The trouble with getting paid along the way: when each interest cheque arrives, the market might offer only lower rates to put it back to work.

definition: Interest rate risk is the risk that changes in market interest rates reduce the value of a bond portfolio or the income from a rate-sensitive asset, with the impact proportional to duration and convexity. Bond prices and yields move inversely, so rising rates impose mark-to-market losses on bondholders even when issuers remain solvent. It is distinct from credit risk and is the dominant risk of high-quality Indian debt funds and government securities holdings.
plainEnglish: The risk that interest rates move against you: when new bonds pay more, old bonds become less valuable. Longer bonds feel it hardest.

definition: Duration gap is the difference between the duration of assets and the duration of liabilities, and it measures the sensitivity of the economic value of equity to a change in interest rates. A positive gap means assets are more rate-sensitive than liabilities, so rising rates reduce net worth, while a negative gap suggests gains when rates rise. It is a standard tool in bank asset-liability management, where the RBI's ALM guidelines frame measurement and monitoring practices.
plainEnglish: The mismatch between when a bank's assets pay off and when its deposits can walk out. If the two sides do not line up, a change in interest rates quietly moves the bank's net worth.

definition: A puttable bond gives the holder the right, at specified dates and prices, to sell the bond back to the issuer before maturity, providing protection against rising rates or deteriorating credit. The embedded put has value to the investor, so puttable bonds offer lower yields than otherwise identical non-puttable bonds. Exercise decisions depend on the prevailing yield and the issuer's credit standing.
plainEnglish: A bond with an escape hatch: if rates rise or the company wobbles, you can hand it back early and get your money.

definition: A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem the bond before maturity at specified call dates and prices, which the issuer typically exercises when interest rates fall and refinancing is cheaper. The call option benefits the issuer at the expense of the investor, so callable bonds carry higher yields than comparable non-callable bonds and their effective duration falls as redemption becomes likely. Indian infrastructure and NBFC issuances frequently include call features.
plainEnglish: A bond the borrower can end early if it suits them, usually by refinancing at a lower rate. You might lose your high-interest bond just when it was most valuable.

definition: A step-up coupon bond pays interest at rates that increase according to a schedule set at issuance, which can compensate investors for uncertainty about credit or inflation over a long tenure. The step pattern is contractual and known in advance, unlike a floating rate note whose payments depend on a market benchmark. The pricing of a step-up bond must account for each future coupon rather than a single level rate.
plainEnglish: A bond whose interest rate rises on a fixed calendar, for example 7% in the early years and 8% later. The raises are promised in advance.

fullName: Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal Securities
definition: STRIPS are zero-coupon securities created by separating the coupon and principal components of eligible government securities so each component trades independently at a discount. Investors use them to construct precise cash flows on chosen future dates with locked-in returns and no reinvestment risk, at the cost of long duration and no interim income. Sovereign strip frameworks define which securities can be decomposed and how the obligations are reconstituted.
plainEnglish: Government bonds sliced apart: each future interest cheque and the final repayment become its own separate mini-investment you can buy at a discount.

definition: Net asset value is the per-unit value of a mutual fund scheme, computed as the scheme's total assets less its liabilities divided by the number of outstanding units, under the valuation norms set out in SEBI's mutual fund regulations. Indian mutual funds declare NAV daily at the prescribed cut-off times, and the units you receive on an investment are allotted at the applicable NAV based on the time your money was cleared. Buying or selling happens at NAV, not at a market-negotiated price.
plainEnglish: The price of one unit of a mutual fund, recalculated every business day. When your ₹10,000 investment buys units at ₹50 each, you get 200 units.

definition: Assets under management is the total market value of all assets that a mutual fund scheme, fund house or asset manager manages on behalf of investors, measured at prevailing market prices. For Indian schemes, monthly AUM is published by AMFI and quarterly disclosures appear in scheme portfolios, and category AUM is often used as a proxy for how crowded a product type has become. AUM grows with net inflows and with market appreciation, so a rising figure does not by itself indicate investor return.
plainEnglish: The total size of the pot all investors have put into a fund or fund house. Big AUM means popularity, not quality.

definition: The expense ratio is the proportion of a scheme's average daily net assets charged annually to meet investment management, administrative, audit, custodian, registrar and marketing expenses. In India the fee components and their overall limits are prescribed by SEBI under the mutual fund regulations, and the ratio is disclosed in the scheme documents and monthly portfolios. Because expenses are charged against the scheme, a higher ratio directly reduces the NAV growth that investors receive.
plainEnglish: The annual fee a fund takes out of your money for managing it. A 1.5% ratio on ₹1 lakh pulls out about ₹1,500 a year, billed invisibly inside the NAV.

definition: The total expense ratio is the all-in annual cost of a mutual fund scheme expressed as a percentage of net assets, comprising recurring expenses permitted under SEBI's mutual fund regulations, whose overall ceiling is banded by scheme size and type. It is the figure investors should compare when selecting between plans, because it bundles management fees, administrative charges and other recurring costs. Regulatory provisions also require surplus amounts above prescribed limits to be credited back to the scheme's income.
plainEnglish: The single number that tells you the total yearly cost of holding a fund, everything included. Compare it like mileage before buying.

definition: An exit load is a charge levied on investors who redeem mutual fund units before a specified holding period, deducted from the redemption proceeds and retained by the scheme's assets. It is designed to discourage frequent trading that would burden long-term investors with transaction costs, and the applicable amount and period are disclosed in the Scheme Information Document and the KIM. In India SEBI has capped the structure and set rules for what the money collected can be used for.
plainEnglish: A fine for leaving a fund too soon. Sell within, say, a year and the fund may keep 1% of your withdrawal.

definition: An entry load was a fee charged when an investor purchased mutual fund units, historically paid to distributors and deducted from the investment amount. SEBI discontinued entry loads on Indian mutual fund schemes in 2009 and subsequent commission structures moved to trail-based recurring payments funded from the scheme's expense ratio, so upfront loads are no longer charged on domestic schemes. The concept remains relevant as a historical reference when reading older product literature.
plainEnglish: An old-style welcome fee taken when you joined a fund. India's regulator scrapped it in 2009, so you no longer pay to get in.

definition: Tracking difference is the simple difference between a fund's return and its benchmark index's return over a period, reflecting the combined effect of fees, transaction costs, cash holdings and dividend treatment. It differs from tracking error, which measures the volatility of that gap rather than its level; a fund can hug its index closely each day yet still trail by the expense ratio over a year. It is a key evaluation tool for Indian index funds and ETFs.
plainEnglish: How far behind the market index a passive fund actually finished. If Nifty rose 10% and the index fund made 9.7%, the tracking difference is 0.3%.

definition: An index fund is a scheme that seeks to replicate the performance of a specified market index by holding its constituents in approximately the same weights, rather than attempting to beat it. Under SEBI's scheme categorisation, index funds are categorised under the equity and other defined categories according to the underlying index, and their costs are typically lower than actively managed peers because portfolio turnover is low. Their deviation from the index is assessed through tracking error and tracking difference.
plainEnglish: A fund that simply copies the market index, holding the same stocks in the same proportion. No manager guessing; you get the market, minus a small fee.

definition: An exchange traded fund is a pooled vehicle whose units are listed and traded on a stock exchange intraday at prices set by demand and supply, unlike open-ended mutual fund units which transact only at end-of-day NAV. Indian ETFs include index, gold and international-exposure products, and creation and redemption by large participants through the fund's authorised mechanism helps keep the market price close to the indicative NAV. Investors bear brokerage and bid-ask spread in addition to the scheme expenses.
plainEnglish: A mutual fund you can buy and sell on the stock exchange like a share, live during market hours. Prices wiggle through the day, so trading costs and pricing matter.

definition: A fund of funds is a mutual fund scheme that invests in units of other mutual fund schemes instead of, or in addition to, directly holding securities, offering diversification across managers and strategies at the cost of an extra layer of expenses. SEBI's categorisation framework limits which categories of domestic or overseas schemes a fund of funds may invest in and requires clear disclosure of the underlying schemes. Its performance depends on the aggregate of the underlying funds' performance net of both levels of costs.
plainEnglish: A basket that holds other mutual funds rather than shares. You get instant spread across funds, and you pay fees at both levels.

definition: An open-ended mutual fund scheme continuously offers units for purchase and redemption at NAV on every business day, with no fixed maturity date, subject to the scheme's exit-load structure. In India most mutual fund categories, including equity, debt, hybrid and solution-oriented schemes, are open-ended under SEBI's categorisation framework. This structure exposes the scheme to ongoing inflows and outflows, which the fund manager must manage alongside the investment mandate.
plainEnglish: A fund that is always open for business: you can put money in or take it out almost any working day, and it never closes on a fixed date.

definition: A close-ended mutual fund scheme raises a fixed corpus during a limited new fund offer period, after which units are not redeemed by the scheme until maturity or as specified; listed close-ended schemes allow investors to exit by selling units on the exchange. SEBI's categorisation rules define the scheme types in which close-ended structures may be launched and prescribe disclosure and listing conditions. Investors who hold until maturity receive proceeds at the scheme's terminal NAV.
plainEnglish: A fund that collects its money once, like an event with a registration window, and then closes its doors until the finish date. Getting out early means selling your units to another investor.

definition: An interval fund is a hybrid structure whose units are open for purchase and redemption only during pre-specified intervals, such as monthly or quarterly windows, rather than continuously or never as with open-ended and close-ended schemes. SEBI's mutual fund regulations set the minimum interval and percentage limits governing when transactions may occur. The structure is intended to blend some exit flexibility with a more stable asset base.
plainEnglish: A fund with scheduled windows for deposits and withdrawals: you can deal with it only during the announced days of the month or quarter.

definition: A systematic investment plan is a facility under which an investor authorises a fixed amount to be invested in a mutual fund scheme at fixed intervals, typically monthly, with units allotted at the applicable NAV on each instalment date. SIPs produce rupee-cost averaging because the same rupee amount buys more units when prices are low and fewer when prices are high, and they remove timing decisions from the investor. Stopping or skipping instalments is permitted subject to the scheme and platform conditions.
plainEnglish: Investing a fixed sum on a fixed date every month, automatically. You buy more units when the market dips and fewer when it is high, without trying to time anything.

definition: A systematic transfer plan moves a lump sum, initially parked in one scheme of a fund house, into another scheme of the same fund house in tranches at fixed intervals. It is commonly used to shift money gradually from a low-volatility debt or liquid scheme into an equity scheme, spreading entry risk while keeping the un-transferred balance productive. The transferor and transferee schemes must satisfy the conditions prescribed by the fund and SEBI's framework.
plainEnglish: Parking your money in a safe fund and arranging for it to be moved into the fund you really want, a slice at a time, automatically.

definition: A systematic withdrawal plan allows an investor to redeem a fixed amount or a fixed number of units from a mutual fund scheme at fixed intervals, with the withdrawal treated as a normal redemption attracting applicable exit loads and capital-gains treatment. It is used to generate regular cash flow from an accumulated corpus, for example in retirement, without annuitising the capital. The sustainability of an SWP depends on the withdrawal rate relative to the scheme's returns and volatility.
plainEnglish: The reverse of a SIP: the fund sends you a fixed sum every month while the rest stays invested. Common for turning a retirement corpus into an income stream.

definition: A direct plan is a mutual fund plan in which the investor deals with the asset management company without an intermediary distributor, so no distribution commission is charged to the scheme and the same portfolio is delivered at a lower expense ratio. NAVs of direct and regular plans of the same scheme therefore differ and diverge over time as expenses compound. SEBI's framework requires both options to be offered and disclosed transparently.
plainEnglish: Buying a fund straight from the fund house and skipping the salesperson's cut. Same portfolio, smaller annual fee, so the direct plan's NAV runs slightly ahead over time.

definition: A regular plan is a mutual fund plan sold through a distributor, with distribution commissions and related expenses borne by the scheme, resulting in a higher expense ratio and a lower NAV than the direct plan of the same scheme. An investor who buys through a distributor pays for advice and transaction assistance implicitly through the expense ratio rather than through an explicit fee. The regular-versus-direct choice is a decision about the value of the intermediary's services against cumulative cost.
plainEnglish: Buying the fund through an agent, whose fees are baked into the fund's annual charges. You get help and hand-holding; you pay for it inside the returns.

definition: Under the growth option of a mutual fund scheme, profits are retained within the scheme rather than distributed, so the NAV compounds and the investor realises value only on redemption. It suits investors seeking capital accumulation because it defers tax incidence until units are sold. The option does not change the portfolio the scheme holds; only the treatment of realised surpluses differs from the distribution option.
plainEnglish: Letting your winnings stay invested and snowball. You do not receive dividends, but the fund's per-unit price grows over time.

definition: IDCW is the option under which a mutual fund scheme distributes part of its realised or accumulated surplus to unit holders, reducing the NAV by the payout amount, which may include a return of part of the investor's capital. SEBI renamed the earlier dividend options as income distribution cum capital withdrawal to make the capital-withdrawal character explicit, and payouts are not guaranteed; some schemes also offer a reinvestment variant. The distributed amount is taxable in the investor's hands according to the applicable rules.
plainEnglish: A fund paying out part of your pot as cash, which shrinks the pot accordingly. It is not extra income appearing from nowhere, sometimes it is literally your own money coming back, with tax.

definition: An asset management company is the SEBI-registered entity that manages the investments of one or more mutual fund schemes under the oversight of the fund's trustees, earning fees within the expense-ratio limits permitted by the regulations. In the Indian three-tier structure, the sponsor promotes the fund, the trustees hold the assets in trust for unit holders, and the AMC runs the day-to-day investment activity. The AMC's obligations, conflict-of-interest standards and reporting duties are prescribed in SEBI's mutual fund regulations.
plainEnglish: The professional fund house that decides what a mutual fund buys and sells, and gets paid a fee from the fund's expenses for doing the job.

definition: The sponsor is the entity that establishes a mutual fund by settling the trust and contributing seed capital and, under SEBI's mutual fund regulations, must meet prescribed eligibility and fit-and-proper conditions. The sponsor appoints the trustee company and, along with the trustees, oversees the appointment of the asset management company. Its role is structural rather than operational: it does not manage the scheme's daily portfolio.
plainEnglish: The parent promoter that sets up the mutual fund, like the founder of a school, while the asset management company is the staff that actually runs the classroom.

definition: The trustee company holds the mutual fund's assets in trust for unit holders and is responsible for protecting their interests, monitoring the asset management company's compliance with the regulations and the scheme documents, and reporting to SEBI.
