Trustees must be independent of the AMC's day-to-day operations and meet prescribed eligibility conditions, and they are required to exercise due diligence on transactions between the fund and related parties. The fund's assets are held by the custodian on behalf of the trustees.
plainEnglish: The independent watchdog standing between you and the fund manager, responsible for making sure your money is where the rules say it should be.

definition: A custodian is a SEBI-registered securities services intermediary that safekeeps a mutual fund's securities, settles its trades and performs corporate-action and income-collection functions for the portfolio. Segregation of the fund's assets from the AMC's own assets is a cornerstone of the mutual fund structure, and the custodian's records evidence that segregation. Custody charges form part of the scheme's permissible expenses.
plainEnglish: The bank vault for a fund's shares. It holds the securities safely, separate from the fund company's own money.

definition: A registrar and transfer agent is a SEBI-registered intermediary appointed by a mutual fund to process investor applications, allot units, maintain the register of unit holders, handle redemptions and switches, and distribute account statements, dividends and other communications. RTAs also service systematic plans and nomination registrations for the schemes they administer. Their records, together with depository records for units held in demat form, evidence an investor's holdings.
plainEnglish: The back office that keeps the investor register for a fund: it records your units, processes your purchases and redemptions, and mails you statements.

definition: The Scheme Information Document is the statutory offer document of a mutual fund scheme, setting out its investment objective, asset allocation pattern, benchmark, risks, fees, exit loads, valuation and redemption policies, and the qualifications of its key personnel. SEBI's regulations prescribe its contents and require updates and addenda to be made public when material changes occur. It is the primary contractual source an investor should examine before subscribing.
plainEnglish: The fund's full rulebook: what it will invest in, what it charges, when it pays out and what risks it warns about. Long, but it is the paperwork that binds the fund.

definition: The Key Information Memorandum is a condensed summary of a mutual fund scheme's Scheme Information Document, covering the essentials of the scheme in a standard format so investors can compare products at a glance. It must accompany the application form and be updated in line with the SID, and it carries the same disclosures on risks, expenses and portfolio policies in abridged form. It does not replace the SID as the governing document.
plainEnglish: The fund's short brochure, a summary of the long rulebook, with the facts you actually need before signing: costs, risks, benchmark, and minimums.

definition: The portfolio turnover ratio measures how actively a scheme's portfolio is traded over a period, computed from the lower of purchases and sales relative to average net assets. A high ratio implies frequent buying and selling, which raises transaction costs borne by unit holders and can reduce tax efficiency for investors, while a low ratio is typical of index and buy-and-hold strategies. Disclosure of turnover is required in Indian scheme portfolios under SEBI's framework.
plainEnglish: How much the fund's portfolio gets reshuffled. A 100% turnover means it effectively replaced everything it owns once in the year.

definition: Cash drag is the reduction in a fund's return caused by holding a portion of assets in cash or near-cash instruments that earn less than the portfolio's other holdings. Funds maintain cash to meet redemptions and pending deployments, and in strongly rising equity markets this buffer lags the rally, while in falling markets it cushions the decline. Large structural cash balances, common in newly launched or illiquid strategies, can be a persistent drag.
plainEnglish: The cost of money sitting idle inside a fund. Cash that is not invested earns little, so it holds back the fund when markets are climbing.

definition: Style drift is the gradual or sudden change in a fund's actual investment style away from its stated mandate or benchmark, for example a large-cap or value-oriented scheme accumulating mid-cap or growth positions. It undermines asset allocation planning because investors end up with unintended exposures and correlated risks across funds. SEBI's categorisation framework, which defines each open-ended scheme category by explicit portfolio constraints, exists partly to curb unapproved drift.
plainEnglish: A fund sliding away from its advertised personality. You bought a conservative large-company fund; over time it starts buying small, racy stocks without changing the label.

definition: A benchmark is the reference index or rate against which a fund's performance and risk are measured, chosen to reflect the scheme's investment universe and mandated in its Scheme Information Document under SEBI's disclosure norms. Indian equity schemes commonly benchmark against broad-market or size- and sector-specific indices administered by NSE Indices and other providers, while debt schemes use short-term rate benchmarks or government-securities indices. Consistent, construction-aware benchmarking is essential because active-return statistics depend on the benchmark selected.
plainEnglish: The yardstick a fund must beat. An index fund's yardstick is its own index; an active fund is judged against the index that best matches what it holds.

definition: A rolling return is computed over many overlapping windows of the same length, for example all three-year periods beginning at each month-end, producing a distribution of outcomes rather than a single number. Rolling analysis reduces the dependence of performance conclusions on arbitrary start dates and reveals the range of experiences an investor could have had. Indian fund platforms and advisers increasingly present rolling-return charts beside point-to-point returns for this reason.
plainEnglish: Average returns computed from thousands of different start dates, so a fund's luck with one particular entry day does not fool you.

definition: A point-to-point return measures the change in NAV between two specific dates, expressed as absolute, annualised or CAGR figures. It is the most common form of performance illustration, but because both endpoints are arbitrary dates chosen by whoever presents the number, it can flatter or penalise a fund depending on market levels at those times. SEBI's performance-advertising rules require standardised disclosure alongside such figures.
plainEnglish: The simple 'from this day to that day' return. Pick a lucky start date and almost any fund looks brilliant.

definition: The category average is the mean return or risk statistic of all schemes within a defined peer group, such as Indian mid-cap equity funds over three years, used to contextualise a single scheme's performance. Its interpretation depends on the peer set's definition, the treatment of funds that closed during the period and the weighting scheme used. Survivorship bias can make published category averages look better than the average investor's realised experience.
plainEnglish: The class scoreboard: how the typical fund in this kind of fund performed. It answers whether 14% is good for this category or merely average.

definition: An arbitrage fund seeks low-risk returns by simultaneously buying securities in the cash market and selling corresponding futures, capturing the price difference between the two legs, and may also deploy in other hedged and cash positions permitted by its mandate. Under SEBI's categorisation it sits in the hybrid group with a defined minimum equity hedging pattern, and its returns are driven by the availability of spreads, which vary with market conditions and derivative pricing. Its tax characterisation can differ from pure debt schemes under the conditions prescribed in the scheme documents and tax law.
plainEnglish: A fund that profits from tiny price gaps between a share and its futures contract, catching them thousands of times. Low drama, modest returns, and useful for parking money expected back soon.

definition: An Equity Linked Savings Scheme is an equity mutual fund category that offers a deduction under s.80C of the Income-tax Act within the overall deduction limit for qualifying investments, in exchange for a statutory lock-in on the units from the date of allotment. SEBI's categorisation prescribes minimum equity investment levels and mandates the lock-in, and dividends or IDCW payouts during the lock-in remain invested. Because of the lock-in, ELSS differs from ordinary open-ended equity funds in redemption flexibility only, not in market risk.
plainEnglish: A tax-saving mutual fund that invests in shares, with a three-year lock-in: put money in within the s.80C limit, claim the tax break, and wait it out.

definition: A lock-in period is a minimum holding period during which an investment cannot be redeemed, imposed by law or by product design, as in the case of ELSS units or tax-saving fixed deposits. The restriction is statutory or contractual and is disclosed in the product documents, and violations are not possible through normal redemption channels. Lock-ins must be matched against the investor's cash-flow needs because they remove the option to exit during market stress.
plainEnglish: A rule that your money must stay put for a set time. ELSS tax-saving funds, for instance, hold your units for three years no matter what the market does.

definition: A new fund offer is the initial subscription period during which a new mutual fund scheme raises money at a fixed offer price before its units are allotted and regular NAV-based dealing begins. The offer period, minimum subscription and allotment mechanics are governed by SEBI's mutual fund regulations and disclosed in the scheme documents. For close-ended schemes, units may be listed on exchanges after allotment so investors have an exit route.
plainEnglish: The launch sale of a brand-new fund: for a limited window you subscribe at a fixed price, then normal daily pricing takes over.

definition: Market capitalisation is the total market value of a company's equity, computed as the number of outstanding shares multiplied by the current market price. For regulatory and fund-classification purposes in India, SEBI prescribes size categories based on full market capitalisation, with large-cap companies those ranked in the top 100, mid-cap those from 101 to 250, and small-cap beyond that, using an industry-maintained ranking list. Market cap reflects the market's estimate of a company's worth, not its intrinsic value or its enterprise value.
plainEnglish: What the stock market thinks a whole company is worth: share price times the number of shares. A ₹500 share with 10 crore shares gives a market cap of ₹5,000 crore.

definition: Free float is the portion of a company's shares available for trading in the market, excluding promoter holdings, strategic stakes and shares subject to lock-in. Index providers weight constituents by free-float market capitalisation so that movements in a company's index weight reflect investable supply rather than total size. A low free float makes a stock prone to sharper moves, including squeeze situations.
plainEnglish: The slice of a company the public can actually buy and sell. Promoter-held shares do not count, so a company whose owners hold almost everything has a small free float.

definition: The price-to-earnings ratio divides a company's share price by its earnings per share, or equivalently its market capitalisation by net profit, and expresses how much investors pay per rupee of annual earnings. Trailing P/E uses the last twelve months of reported earnings, while forward P/E uses analyst estimates, which introduces forecast error. A high P/E may reflect growth expectations, temporary earnings weakness or overvaluation, and its level is only meaningful relative to an industry, history and interest-rate context.
plainEnglish: The years-of-profits price tag: a P/E of 20 means the market is paying ₹20 for every ₹1 the company earns each year. Expensive-looking numbers can be justified by fast growth, or not.

definition: The price-to-book ratio divides share price by book value per share, where book value is the accounting net worth of the company attributable to equity holders. It is most informative for asset-heavy companies such as banks and manufacturers, where book value has close economic meaning, and least informative for businesses whose chief assets are intangibles. A P/B below one invites questions about the quality of stated book value.
plainEnglish: The price tag compared with the company's accounting net worth. A bank with a 0.8 P/B is priced below its stated balance-sheet value; above 1 means you are paying a premium to the books.

definition: EV/EBITDA divides enterprise value, being market capitalisation plus debt minus cash, by earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. It compares total claims on the business against pre-financing operating profitability, making it a more capital-structure-neutral measure than the P/E ratio. It is widely used in Indian valuations and takeover analyses, and is arguably overused for businesses with high capital expenditure where depreciation is an economic cost.
plainEnglish: A fuller version of the P/E test: you count the company's debt in the price, and compare against operating profit before accounting deductions, so companies with different borrowing are comparable.

definition: Dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the share price, expressing the cash return a shareholder receives relative to the cost of the share. It changes inversely with price, so a falling price raises the yield on the declared dividend, and it can be misleading when a dividend is a one-off or includes special payouts. In India, dividends declared by domestic companies are taxable in the shareholder's hands as income under the law, so the tax has to be considered when comparing yields across products.
plainEnglish: The cash your shares pay you each year as a percentage of their price. A ₹4 dividend on a ₹100 share is a 4% yield; remember the tax slice before comparing with a bank deposit.

definition: Return on equity measures net profit after tax as a percentage of shareholders' equity, tracking how efficiently a company turns shareholders' capital into distributable profit. It is decomposable into margin, asset turnover and leverage, so a high ROE may come from heavy borrowing rather than operating excellence. Sustained high ROE without leverage is a commonly used marker of quality in Indian equity analysis.
plainEnglish: The return the company earns on the owners' money. A 16% ROE means every ₹100 of shareholders' capital generated about ₹16 of profit that year.

definition: Return on capital employed measures operating profit before interest and tax as a percentage of capital employed, comprising shareholders' funds plus long-term debt less intangibles as defined in the analysis. Because it uses pre-interest profit, it judges the productivity of all capital regardless of how the company is financed, making it useful for comparing firms with different leverage. A company creates value when ROCE exceeds its weighted average cost of capital.
plainEnglish: How hard all the money in the business, whether the owners' or the lenders', is working. When it beats the cost of borrowing that money, the company is genuinely creating wealth.

definition: Earnings per share is a company's profit after tax attributable to equity shareholders divided by the weighted average number of shares outstanding during the period, and it is required disclosure in Indian financial statements under accounting standards. Diluted EPS additionally assumes conversion of all potential shares such as options and convertible securities, giving the most conservative figure. EPS growth does not automatically translate into shareholder value if it requires disproportionate capital.
plainEnglish: The company's yearly profit sliced by each share. If it earned ₹50 crore with 5 crore shares outstanding, EPS is ₹10 per share.
formula: EPS = \frac{\text{Profit after Tax} - \text{Preference Dividends}}{\text{Weighted Average Shares}}

definition: Promoter holding is the proportion of a listed company's shares held by its promoter group as disclosed in the quarterly shareholding pattern filed with the exchanges under SEBI's listing obligations and disclosure requirements. Company law and listing rules prescribe minimum public shareholding that promoters must leave outside, designed to keep a floor of tradable ownership. Promoter concentration affects governance: very high holdings can entrench control, while very low holdings can signal weak confidence.
plainEnglish: How much of the company its founders and the family still own. A large chunk means founders are invested alongside you; consistent selling is a signal worth noticing.

definition: Promoter pledging occurs when promoters use their shares as collateral for loans, typically to fund personal or group obligations, with the pledged shares disclosed in the shareholding-pattern filings made to the exchanges. A high pledged proportion raises the risk that forced sales by lenders will depress the stock price or transfer control if loans are not serviced. The disclosure regime requires periodic reporting of encumbered promoter holdings, making it a standard governance red flag screen.
plainEnglish: Founders putting their own shares up as security for loans. If the loan sours, lenders can sell those shares into the market, which can hammer the price.

definition: Circuit limits are exchange-imposed daily price bands that stop a security from moving beyond a specified percentage in either direction during a trading session, after which trading in that security halts or continues only within the band under exchange rules. The bands may be tightened or widened based on surveillance concerns, and market-wide circuit breakers halt the whole market on extreme index moves at prescribed thresholds. The mechanism caps single-day disorderly moves but does not prevent multi-day repricing.
plainEnglish: Speed bumps imposed by the exchange: a stock is not allowed to rise or fall more than a set percentage in a day. If panic persists, the stock just hits the same wall the next day.

definition: The trade-to-trade segment was a trading mechanism in which every purchase had to result in delivery and every sale had to be backed by holdings, with no intraday squaring-off, imposed on securities by way of surveillance. It was designed to discourage speculation in low-quality or manipulated counters, and it has been progressively replaced or supplemented by other surveillance measures such as periodic call auctions and additional surveillance frameworks. Being placed in such a segment is itself a caution signal about a stock's trading quality.
plainEnglish: A trading penalty box: shares put in this list must be bought and held for real, with no day-trading allowed, usually because regulators distrust the way they are being traded.

definition: Group A and group B were BSE's traditional equity classifications, with group A comprising the largest, most liquid and blue-chip companies and group B the broader set of ordinary scrips, alongside later categories used for specialised and vigil stocks. The groupings historically influenced settlement and eligibility conventions, and are still referred to colloquially when describing a stock's pedigree and liquidity. Modern classification increasingly relies on market-cap tiers and surveillance lists rather than the legacy groups.
plainEnglish: An old stock-market tier system: Group A names were the blue chips, Group B the crowded middle. Like a supermarket putting premium items on the top shelf.

definition: In a public issue conducted through book building, the price band is the range between a floor and cap within which investors may submit bids, set by the issuer in consultation with the lead managers in accordance with SEBI's issue regulations. Bids below the floor or above the cap are invalid, and the final issue price is discovered from the bids within the band. The same term is also used for exchange circuit bands in secondary trading, so context matters.
plainEnglish: The allowed price window for bidding in a new share sale, for example ₹90 to ₹100. You choose the price you will pay inside that window; the company settles on the final price from the demand.

definition: Book building is the process by which an issuer discovers the price of a public offer by collecting bids at various prices within a band from qualified institutional buyers, non-institutional investors and retail investors, with allocations governed by SEBI's issue of capital and disclosure requirements regulations. The portion reserved for each investor category, the treatment of anchor investors and the allotment logic are prescribed, and the final price may be the floor, cap or a discovered level. Bids are demand indications, and revision and withdrawal windows apply during the offer period.
plainEnglish: A price auction for a new share issue: the company sets a range, investors say how many shares they will buy at what price, and the final price emerges from the bids.

definition: An initial public offering is a company's first sale of equity shares to the public, after which the shares are listed and traded on one or more recognised stock exchanges under SEBI's regulations. The offer may comprise a fresh issue of shares, an offer for sale by existing holders, or both, with proceeds from the fresh issue going to the company. Listing transforms a private security into a liquid, continuously priced asset but does not guarantee that the offer price was attractive.
plainEnglish: A private company's debut on the stock market, selling shares to any investor for the first time. You buy at the offer price, and from listing day onward the market decides what they are really worth.

definition: A follow-on public offer is a subsequent public offering of shares by a company already listed, used to raise additional capital or to allow existing holders to divest, and conducted under the same SEBI issue regulations as an IPO. It differs from a rights issue because the offer is open to the general public rather than reserved for existing shareholders. FPOs can be fixed-price or book-built and must satisfy eligibility and disclosure conditions.
plainEnglish: A second round of public selling by a company already on the exchange, open to everyone, usually to fund expansion or let early backers sell.

definition: An offer for sale is a mechanism under SEBI's regulations through which existing shareholders, such as promoters, private-equity investors or the government, sell shares to the public through the exchange platform, without the company issuing new shares or receiving any proceeds. Retail investors receive a defined reservation portion and may place bids at or below the floor price, with the clearing price determined by demand. Because proceeds accrue to the selling shareholders, an OFS changes ownership distribution rather than funding the business.
plainEnglish: A sale where existing owners, not the company, sell their shares to you. The money goes to them, and the company gets nothing.

definition: A rights issue offers new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their current holding for a defined period, usually at a price below the market price, giving them the right to maintain their ownership share. The entitlement can typically be renounced in favour of others, and the price, ratio and record date are set out in the letter of offer under SEBI and company-law requirements. Not subscribing means accepting dilution of one's ownership stake.
plainEnglish: The company offering existing owners first refusal on new shares, often at a discount, so they can protect their slice of the pie. Skip it and your slice shrinks.

definition: A bonus issue is the allotment of additional equity shares to existing shareholders free of cost, funded by capitalising the company's reserves rather than by cash subscription. The number of shares increases proportionately while the market price adjusts downward on the ex-date so that a holder's total value is unchanged at the moment of allotment, apart from tax considerations. It is economically distinct from a dividend because no cash leaves the company.
plainEnglish: Free extra shares, funded from the company's saved-up reserves: own one share and you might get one more, but its price roughly halves to keep the value of your holding the same.

definition: A stock split divides each existing share into multiple shares, lowering the face value and the market price proportionately, so the investor's total value is unchanged and their number of shares increases. It improves affordability and granularity for small investors but does not alter market capitalisation or economic ownership. In India, a split is implemented under company-law provisions with exchange intimation and has an ex-date effect on the price series.
plainEnglish: Chopping one expensive share into several cheaper ones. Two ₹1,500 shares become four ₹750 shares: same value, easier to trade.

definition: A buyback is a purchase of its own shares by a company, either through a tender offer to all shareholders or from the open market under the framework of the Companies Act and SEBI's buyback regulations, subject to limits on size and resources. Cash returns to participating shareholders and the outstanding share count falls, mechanically raising earnings per share for the remaining holders. The tax treatment of buyback proceeds depends on the applicable law and has changed across regimes, so it should be checked for the relevant year.
plainEnglish: A company using its spare cash to buy part of itself from investors, either by asking them to sell or by buying on the market. It shrinks the number of shares and can boost the value of those left.

definition: Delisting is the permanent removal of a company's shares from stock-exchange trading, either voluntarily at the initiative of promoters or involuntarily by exchange action for compliance failures. Voluntary delisting typically requires a reverse book-building process in which public shareholders tender shares and a discovered price must be accepted or the attempt fails, governed by SEBI's delisting regulations. Once delisted, the securities lose their continuous market and exit options narrow to negotiated or tribunal-mediated routes.
plainEnglish: Taking a company's shares off the stock exchange for good. Owners are offered a buy-out price; if enough do not agree, the attempt fails.

definition: A demerger is a scheme of arrangement under company law by which a company transfers one or more of its businesses or undertakings to another entity, with shareholders of the demerged company receiving shares of the resulting or transferee company. The division is implemented through the tribunal approval process, and the cost of acquisition of the original shares is apportioned between the resulting entities for capital-gains purposes as prescribed. Post-demerger, investors hold stakes in separate businesses with independent economics and risks.
plainEnglish: Splitting one company into two: if you owned the parent, you automatically get shares of the spun-off business too, like a pizza cut in half, each half with its own flavour.

definition: A corporate action is any event initiated by a listed company that materially affects its securities, including dividends and IDCW, bonus issues, splits, rights issues, buybacks, mergers, demergers and capital restructuring. Companies must announce such events to the exchanges, and the price and holdings records are adjusted around the ex-date and record date. Investors need corporate-action awareness because unclaimed entitlements can lapse and because cost-basis adjustments affect their tax computation.
plainEnglish: Anything a company does that changes your shares or pays you money: dividends, splits, bonuses, buybacks. The exchange adjusts prices and accounts automatically around the event date.

definition: The ex-date is the trading date from which a security no longer carries entitlement to an announced corporate action, so a buyer purchasing on or after that date does not receive the dividend, bonus shares, rights or other benefit. The exchange adjusts the reference price on the ex-date to reflect the value of the entitlement leaving the security. Settlement timelines determine how many days before the record date the ex-date falls.
plainEnglish: The cut-off trading day for a company handout: buy before it and the dividend or bonus is yours; buy on or after it and you have missed the boat.

definition: The record date is the date on which the company determines the names of shareholders entitled to a corporate action, based on settled holdings in the depository system or the register of members. Because of settlement cycles, the corresponding ex-date falls earlier, and trades must settle in the buyer's account by the record date for entitlement. Companies announce record dates to the exchanges along with the corporate action terms.
plainEnglish: The eligibility day: whoever is on the register on that date gets the payout. Because trades take days to settle, you must buy a few days earlier.

definition: Insider trading is dealing in a listed company's securities while in possession of unpublished price-sensitive information, or communicating such information, both prohibited under SEBI's prohibition of insider trading regulations. The regime imposes disclosure obligations on designated persons, restrictions on trading during closure of trading windows, and severe civil and criminal consequences for violations. It harms market integrity by transferring returns from uninformed investors to those with privileged access.
plainEnglish: Trading on secrets you were given because of your position, like a manager buying shares knowing good results before they are announced. Illegal, with heavy penalties.

definition: A bulk deal is a transaction in a listed security whose quantity exceeds the percentage of the company's total listed shares prescribed by the stock exchanges for single-day disclosure, and it must be reported to the exchange daily with the identity of the buyer and seller. Bulk deals occur through normal order-book trading and their disclosure allows the market to see unusual concentrations of buying or selling. Regulation of such disclosures aims to reduce information asymmetry regarding significant position changes.
plainEnglish: A purchase or sale so large that the exchange forces the names behind it into the open at the end of the day, so everyone can see who was loading up or dumping.

definition: A block deal is a large negotiated transaction executed through a dedicated exchange window during specified session timings, at a price within the range prescribed relative to prevailing prices, with the minimum trade size and disclosure norms set by the exchanges. It allows institutional and strategic holders to move significant quantities without disrupting the ordinary order book. Trade details are published by the exchanges after the window, making the identity of large transactors visible.
plainEnglish: A separate, scheduled counter on the exchange for big trades: institutions swap large parcels of shares at one negotiated price without shaking the normal market.

definition: Forensic accounting applies investigative techniques to financial statements to detect misstatement, manipulation or fraud, examining revenue recognition, related-party dealings, cash-flow quality, receivable ageing and unusual ratios for red flags. In Indian equity research it is used to question reported numbers before they are restated or discovered by regulators. Common warning patterns include profits without matching operating cash flow, related-party circularity and sudden auditor resignations.
plainEnglish: Detective work on company accounts. It looks past the pretty numbers for tricks and warning signs, the way you would check for hidden clauses in a contract.

definition: A related-party transaction is a dealing between a company and a party with which it has a relationship of control, common interest or key-management connection, as defined in company law and accounting standards. Indian law requires such transactions to be at arm's length in ordinary course and, when material, to receive audit-committee and shareholder approval with disclosures under SEBI's listing regulations. Certainty of arm's-length pricing is central to judging whether minority shareholders are being advantaged or exploited.
plainEnglish: A company doing business with its own extended family, like a subsidiary or the promoter's other firm. Legal, but only if the pricing is fair and the deals are transparently disclosed.

definition: An employee stock option plan grants employees the option to buy company shares at a set exercise price after a vesting schedule, aligning employee incentives with shareholder value, and is governed for listed companies by SEBI's regulations on share-based employee benefits. When exercised, new shares are issued or existing shares transferred, causing dilution that existing investors should factor in. The perquisite value on exercise is taxable under the Income-tax Act, with specific mechanics for eligible start-ups.
plainEnglish: A perk that lets employees buy company shares at a fixed price, usually cheaper than the market, as a reward for staying and performing. Exercising it adds shares and thus dilutes everyone else slightly.

definition: A restricted stock unit is a promise to give an employee company shares at no cost or a nominal cost once vesting conditions, typically service tenure plus performance, are satisfied, and they are used heavily by new-age Indian technology companies. Unlike an option, an RSU does not require the employee to pay an exercise price and its value tracks the share price directly. Awards and their vesting affect the share count and must be disclosed by listed companies in their filings.
plainEnglish: Shares promised by the company and delivered free once you fulfil the waiting conditions. Like an ESOP, but with no purchase price to pay, so the whole share value is the reward.

definition: Sweat equity shares are shares issued by a company to directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash, in recognition of know-how, intellectual property or other value addition, under the conditions prescribed in the Companies Act and rules. Issuance requires specified approvals, valuation and lock-in conditions that restrict early sale of the shares. It is a way to compensate founders and key contributors without cash outflow, at the cost of dilution to other shareholders.
plainEnglish: Shares handed out in exchange for brains and effort rather than cash, which is why they are literally called sweat equity. They come with a lock-in so recipients cannot cash out immediately.

definition: Advance tax is the pay-as-you-earn mechanism under which income tax for the year is discharged in instalments during the year on income not covered by tax deducted at source, based on the taxpayer's own estimate of annual income. For individuals, instalments fall due quarterly on prescribed dates, and interest is charged for shortfall or default in each instalment. Salaried persons with no other significant income usually have the whole liability met through salary TDS and need not pay advance tax.
plainEnglish: Paying your tax in four instalments through the year instead of one big bill in July. If you have rent, freelance fees or capital gains beyond salaried TDS, you are expected to keep paying as you go.

definition: Tax deducted at source is the system under which the payer of specified incomes, such as salary, interest, rent, professional fees or commission, deducts tax at prescribed rates and deposits it with the government, issuing the payee a certificate of deduction. The deducted amount is credited to the payee's tax account and reflected in the tax-credit statements, to be set off against final liability. Rates and exemption thresholds are specified in the Act and revised by successive Finance Acts, and nil or lower deduction certificates may be applied for where the actual liability is lower.
plainEnglish: The payer acts as a tax collector: part of your salary, interest or fees is paid to the government on your behalf before you get it. You then settle the difference when you file your return.

definition: Tax collected at source is a mechanism under which the seller of specified goods or services, or a remitter in the case of prescribed foreign-exchange transactions, collects tax from the buyer or remitter at prescribed rates and deposits it with reference to the buyer's identity. The collected amount appears in the buyer's or remitter's tax-credit records and is available for set-off against final tax liability for individuals, subject to the conditions in the Act. Thresholds, rates and the categories covered have changed over time and are prescribed in the law and Finance Acts.
plainEnglish: Like TDS in reverse: when you buy certain things or send money abroad, the seller or bank collects a slice as advance tax and deposits it against your name.

definition: Surcharge is an additional charge on income tax levied at graduated rates when total income exceeds prescribed thresholds, with the rate depending on the level of income and, for certain capital-gains provisions, capped at a lower slab. Surcharge applies over and above the normal tax and is itself subject to cess, and the Act provides marginal relief so that crossing a surcharge threshold does not reduce the taxpayer's net income. For income taxed under the special concessional capital-gains provisions, the maximum surcharge is limited, which affects the effective rate on such gains.
plainEnglish: A wealth-tier top-up on tax: earn above certain levels and the government adds a percentage on top of your tax bill, softened by rules that stop the extra slab from eating all your gain.

definition: The health and education cess is a levy charged as a percentage of the aggregate of income tax and surcharge, earmarked for health and education spending, currently levied at four percent as prescribed by the Finance Act. It applies across income categories, including capital gains taxed at special rates, so effective rates of tax are materially above the headline rate. Because it is computed after surcharge, its rupee impact is larger for high-income taxpayers.
plainEnglish: A four-percent top-up on your total tax, added automatically, which funds health and education programmes. Because it compounds on top of surcharge, high earners feel it more.

definition: The rebate is a direct reduction of income tax available to resident individuals with total income up to the prescribed limit, designed to shield lower-income taxpayers from the full slab burden; its amount, limit and interaction with special-rate incomes are specified in the Act and revised by Finance Acts. The rebate is not a deduction from income: it applies after computing tax on total income. For incomes slightly above the limit, the Act provides marginal relief so the additional tax does not exceed the additional income.
plainEnglish: A discount applied to your final tax bill, not your income, for people earning below a set level. Earn just above it and relief rules soften the jump.

definition: Marginal relief limits the tax payable when income marginally exceeds a threshold for a higher slab, surcharge band or the rebate limit, capping the incremental tax at the incremental income in the specified manner. It operates through formulas prescribed in the Finance Act and appears both around the rebate zone and around surcharge thresholds. Without it, a rupee more of income could cost many times that amount in tax.
plainEnglish: A fairness cushion at slab borders: if crossing a threshold would raise your tax by more than the extra money you earned, the law trims the tax back.

definition: Capital gains are profits arising from the transfer of a capital asset, taxed under the Income-tax Act and classified as short-term or long-term by the holding period, with different rates and exemptions for different asset classes. Gains on listed equity and equity-oriented funds above the prescribed annual exemption carry concessional rates under the special provisions, while debt-oriented mutual funds acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are governed by s.50AA, which treats gains as short-term regardless of holding period, ending the earlier indexation benefit. The character of the gain flows from the character of the asset, so the same transaction can be taxed very differently depending on what was sold.
plainEnglish: Profit made when you sell an asset at a higher price than you bought it, taxed in different ways depending on what you sold and how long you held it.

definition: Short-term capital gains arise on the transfer of a capital asset held for not more than the prescribed holding period, which is 12 months for listed equity shares and equity-oriented fund units and longer for other assets. Listed-equity short-term gains specified under the law are taxed at a concessional flat rate rather than normal slab rates, and no annual exemption applies to them. The applicable rate has been changed by successive Finance Acts, and the surcharge on such gains is capped at a lower maximum than for ordinary income.
plainEnglish: Profit from selling an asset quick enough to classify as short-term, which is taxed at its own fixed rate for shares and equity funds.

definition: Long-term capital gains arise when a capital asset is held beyond the prescribed holding period, generally more than 12 months for listed equity and equity-oriented funds and more than 24 months for unlisted shares and immovable property. For listed equity and equity-oriented funds where securities transaction tax has been paid, gains under the special provision are taxed at the prescribed rate on the amount exceeding the aggregate annual exemption, without indexation, for transfers on or after 23 July 2024. For other assets, the treatment varies between the prescribed flat rates and indexation regimes, and legal advice for the specific asset and date is essential.
plainEnglish: Profit on an asset you kept long-term. Share gains above a yearly exemption are taxed at a special lower rate; property and gold have their own rules.

definition: The holding period is the duration for which a capital asset is held before transfer, measured from the date of acquisition to the date of transfer under the rules in the Income-tax Act, and it determines whether a gain is long-term or short-term. The thresholds differ by asset class, with listed securities generally using a shorter period than unlisted shares and immovable property. Special rules govern the starting date for assets acquired through gifts, inheritance, bonus issues, rights issues and corporate restructurings.
plainEnglish: How long you owned the thing before selling, which decides whether your profit gets the kinder long-term tax treatment.

definition: Indexation adjusts the purchase cost of a capital asset for inflation between acquisition and sale using the cost inflation index, reducing the taxable capital gain; it is available only for asset classes and periods for which the statute permits it, and the Finance Act 2024 restricted or withdrew it for several categories with effect from 23 July 2024. For debt-oriented mutual funds, indexation was withdrawn for units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 under s.50AA, which treats such gains as short-term, while a resident individual's option of the 20% rate with indexation for land and buildings acquired before 23 July 2024 was preserved by the amending legislation. Any current computation must follow the law applicable to the asset and transfer date.
plainEnglish: Beefing up your purchase price to account for inflation, so the tax is charged only on the real gain. India has been chipping away at where this benefit applies, so the date you bought matters enormously.

definition: The cost inflation index is a series notified annually by the central government, with a base year and values for each financial year, used to convert historical acquisition costs into inflation-adjusted terms for capital-gains computations where indexation is permitted. The index for the year of transfer divided by the index for the year of acquisition gives the multiplier applied to the original cost. Because indexation has been restricted for later acquisitions in several asset categories, the CII is now relevant mainly where the law still allows it.
plainEnglish: A government-published price-level table, one number per year. Divide the year you sold by the year you bought and you know how much to inflate your purchase cost.

definition: Set-off allows a taxpayer to adjust a loss from one source or head against income from another in the same year to the extent permitted, for example capital losses against capital gains, while certain losses such as those from speculative business cannot be set against other heads. Unabsorbed losses may be carried forward for the prescribed number of years, capital losses for up to eight assessment years, against the same head of income, and carry-forward is generally available only if the return is filed within the due date. The character of the loss matters: short-term capital losses, for instance, can be set against both short-term and long-term gains, while long-term losses cannot be set against short-term gains.
plainEnglish: Matching your losers against your winners to shrink the taxable total. If the losses are bigger than the gains this year, you can bank them for future years, provided you filed your return on time.

definition: Tax-loss harvesting is the deliberate realisation of paper losses on investments to offset realised gains elsewhere in the portfolio, reducing current taxable income, with the option of repurchasing similar exposure if the investor's view on the asset is unchanged. In India it is most commonly used for equity and equity-oriented fund units in the s.112A regime, where gains above the annual exemption are taxed at the prescribed rate, and it interacts with the set-off and carry-forward rules and with short-term versus long-term loss characterisation. Transaction costs, exit loads and the risk of a wrong-market entry timing can erode the tax saving.
plainEnglish: Selling something at a loss on purpose before year-end so its loss cancels tax on your winners. You can often buy the position back and keep it.

definition: Tax residency determines which country has the primary right to tax a person's income, and for India it is based on the number of days of stay in the financial year plus conditions about prior-year presence and residence elsewhere, as prescribed in the Income-tax Act. A resident is taxed on global income, while a non-resident is taxed only on Indian-source income, and residency can differ from citizenship and from visa status. Days-of-stay counts, deemed-resident rules for very high-income non-residents and tie-breaker rules under tax treaties must all be examined together.
plainEnglish: The test for which country you owe tax to, decided mostly by how many days a year you actually spend in India. Living abroad but spending months in India can change your status.

definition: An RNOR is an individual who satisfies the basic residency test for the year but is not ordinarily resident under the additional conditions prescribed in the Income-tax Act, which focus on presence and non-residence in preceding years. An RNOR is taxed on income that accrues or arises in India and on foreign income only if it derives from a business controlled in, or a profession set up in, India, which is narrower than the global-income basis applying to ordinarily resident persons. The RNOR status is transitional and typically lasts for a limited number of years after arrival or return.
plainEnglish: A part-time resident for tax: you are more resident than a visitor but less than a full resident, so most foreign income is not taxed here during your transition years.

definition: A DTAA is a bilateral treaty between two countries allocating taxing rights over different classes of income, such as dividends, interest, royalties, capital gains and salaries, and prescribing relief where both countries would otherwise tax the same income. India has a network of such agreements, and relief may be granted by exemption with the source country taxing, or by credit in the country of residence for tax paid abroad, depending on the treaty article. Claiming treaty benefits generally requires evidence of tax residency such as a TRC and, where prescribed, a no-permanent-establishment or beneficial-ownership declaration.
plainEnglish: A pact between countries so the same income is not fully taxed twice, dividing who gets to charge you and at what rate.

definition: A foreign tax credit reduces Indian tax liability by the tax already paid to a foreign jurisdiction on income that is also taxable in India, computed under the rules in the Income-tax Act read with the applicable treaty, and normally limited to the Indian tax attributable to that income. Different credit rules apply to foreign taxes deducted at source from dividends, interest and capital gains realised on foreign investments. Credits must be supported by foreign tax payment evidence and claimed through the prescribed procedural route.
plainEnglish: The relief that stops you paying twice: tax already paid abroad is knocked off what you would owe India on the same income.

definition: Form 67 is the prescribed form for claiming a foreign tax credit on foreign income under the Income-tax Act, filed electronically along with evidence of the foreign tax deduction and proof of payment, typically before the return of income is filed. Timely filing is important because delay can jeopardise the credit unless the return is updated or the prescribed condonation route is used. Flighty omissions in supposedly simple cases, such as foreign dividend withholding on US-listed holdings, are a common reason Indian investors lose credits.
plainEnglish: The official paperwork you must submit to claim back the tax another country already withheld on your foreign investment income, and you have to file it before your return.

definition: The Annual Information Statement is a consolidated statement on the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal that presents a taxpayer's financial transactions and events reported by various reporting entities during a financial year, including interest, dividends, securities transactions and foreign remittances, with feedback options for inaccurate items. It supplements the tax-credit information in the simpler statement that primarily shows TDS and TCS, giving a fuller picture for reconciliation before filing. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, which takes effect from 1 April 2026, forms and statements have been reorganised, and the AIS concept continues in substance under the newer framework.
plainEnglish: The tax department's own file on you: a long list of all the interest, dividends and transactions banks, brokers and others have reported in your name, so nothing gets forgotten when you file.

definition: Form 26AS is the annual consolidated tax statement showing tax deducted at source, tax collected at source, advance and self-assessment tax paid, refunds received and specified high-value financial transactions, which the taxpayer can view and download from the e-filing portal or through the tax-information service. It serves as the evidence of tax credits available against the taxpayer's assessed liability, and mismatches between it and the return commonly trigger intimations. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, effective from 1 April 2026, the statement is carried forward in substance with renumbered forms.
plainEnglish: Your official tax receipt record: everything already deducted or paid toward your taxes shows up here, and you check it before filing so nothing is missed.

definition: Presumptive taxation is a simplification under which specified taxpayers, such as small businesses and eligible professionals, can declare income at a prescribed percentage of turnover or gross receipts, or on a presumptive basis for certain transport operators, instead of maintaining detailed books and computing actual profit. Choosing it limits the benefit of deductions and can bind the taxpayer to the framework for subsequent years unless the exit conditions are met. The object is to reduce compliance burden for small assessees within the turnover limits prescribed by the law.
plainEnglish: A shortcut for small businesses: declare profit as a set percentage of your sales, no detailed accounting required.

definition: Minimum alternate tax is a provision requiring companies that claim deductions or incentive-driven reductions such that their normal tax liability falls below a prescribed percentage of book profit to pay tax on that minimum book-profit base, computed under the Income-tax Act. Tax paid as MAT can be carried forward and set off against normal tax in later years within the limits prescribed, providing relief against the anti-abuse nature of the charge. Rates and applicability are subject to successive Finance Act changes and to the transitional rules under the Income-tax Act, 2025.
plainEnglish: A floor under company tax: even a company with clever deductions pays at least a minimum slice based on its accounting profits, with credit for later years.

definition: Alternate minimum tax is the parallel floor for non-corporate assessees, such as individuals, HUFs and firms claiming specified deductions, under which adjusted total income including add-back of the deductions is taxed at a prescribed rate if it exceeds the threshold in the Act. AMT credit arising on payment can be set off against normal tax in subsequent years within the prescribed window. As with MAT, the regime interacts with the taxpayer's broader incentive claims and applies only above the prescribed adjusted-total-income limit.
plainEnglish: The same minimum-tax floor as companies have, but for individuals and firms who try to drive their taxable income very low using deductions.

definition: Clubbing of income is the rule under the Income-tax Act by which income transferred to certain related persons, or earned by them from assets transferred without adequate consideration, is included in the transferor's total income, preventing diversion of income to lower-taxed family members. It covers transfers to spouses, the income derived from assets gifted to a minor child subject to limited exceptions, and certain transactions with son's wife and other specified relatives. Clubbing determines whose slab rates apply, and it differs from aggregation merely for rate purposes.
plainEnglish: An anti-avoidance rule: if you park your money with your spouse or child to dodge tax, the income is still counted as yours.

definition: A Hindu undivided family is treated as a separate taxable person under the Income-tax Act, comprising all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, with its own PAN, exemption threshold and slab structure, and governed in its civil law aspects by local family law. Income received by an HUF from ancestral property or family business is taxed in its own hands, and assets gifted into the HUF raise clubbing and character questions for both the member and the family. Partition, karta representation and coparcener rights shape how HUF finances are managed.
plainEnglish: A family treated as its own taxpayer: the family pool of property and business has its own tax number and its income is taxed separately from any member's.

definition: India does not levy a separate gift tax, but gifts received by a person in excess of the prescribed aggregate annual limit are taxed as income from other sources under s.56(2)(x) of the Income-tax Act, subject to exclusions for gifts from relatives, on the occasion of marriage, under a will or inheritance among others. Gifts in kind are valued under prescribed rules and the recipient, not the donor, bears the tax. The regime is aimed at detecting unaccounted transfers while keeping genuine family transfers out of charge.
plainEnglish: Free money is taxable if it is big enough, with generous exceptions. Gifts from close relatives and wedding gifts stay tax-free; surprises from strangers do not.

definition: Section 112A is the special provision under the Income-tax Act that taxes long-term capital gains on listed equity shares, equity-oriented mutual fund units and units of business trusts where securities transaction tax is paid, on the amount of gains exceeding a prescribed aggregate annual exemption for a resident individual or HUF. For transfers on or after 23 July 2024 the rate is 12.5% without indexation, following the Finance Act 2024 changes, and grandfathering rules apply to assets acquired before 31 January 2018. Losses on s.112A assets have restricted set-off, and their interaction with loss characterisation and the annual exemption requires care.
plainEnglish: The rulebook for taxing long-term gains on shares and equity funds: 12.5% beyond the yearly exemption of gains, no inflation adjustment, with special historical rules for very old holdings.

definition: Securities transaction tax is a transaction-level levy collected on specified transactions in listed equity shares, equity-oriented mutual fund units and exchange-traded derivatives, payable by the buyer, the seller or both, at rates prescribed by the Finance Act. Where STT has been paid, gains on listed equity attract the concessional capital-gains rates under the special provisions; conversely, exemptions and concessional treatment are conditioned on the STT payment. Since STT is charged on the value of the transaction rather than on profit, it applies even on loss-making trades.
plainEnglish: A tiny tax built into every stock-market trade, collected by the exchange itself. It is what qualifies your gains for the lower share-market capital-gains rates.

definition: A futures contract is a standardised exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell an underlying asset at a predetermined price on a specified future date, marked to market daily and guaranteed by the exchange's clearing corporation. Indian index and stock futures are governed by SEBI's framework and exchange contract specifications, including lot sizes and expiry conventions revised from time to time. Positions may be held to expiry or squared off earlier, with the daily settlement of gains and losses through the margin account.
plainEnglish: A binding deal to trade something at a fixed price on a future date, with both sides putting up margin. You can close it before the date and take the profit or loss.

definition: An option is a contract giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at a stated strike price by a specified expiry, in exchange for a premium paid to the seller. SEBI's framework governs the Indian exchange-traded option market, including contract specifications, position limits and margin requirements. Because the buyer's loss is limited to the premium while the seller's obligation is potentially much larger, the risk profiles of the two sides are fundamentally asymmetric.
plainEnglish: A paid-up choice: you buy the right to make a deal at a set price, and you can simply walk away if the deal would be bad. Whoever sells you that right sits on the other side of the risk.

definition: A call option gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike price on or before expiry, so its value rises as the underlying price rises above the strike. The buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid, while the seller, who receives the premium, bears the risk of delivering the underlying at the strike when the market price is higher. Indian index and stock call options trade in standardised series on the exchanges.
plainEnglish: The right to buy something at today's agreed price even if the market price later runs higher. If it falls instead, you just do not use your right and lose only the fee you paid.

definition: A put option gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying at the strike price on or before expiry, so its value rises as the underlying price falls below the strike. It functions as portfolio insurance when held against underlying holdings, with a known maximum cost equal to the premium. The seller of the put receives the premium but accepts the obligation to buy the underlying at the strike if the buyer exercises.
plainEnglish: The right to sell something at your agreed price even if the market has crashed. Like an insurance policy on your shares, paid for upfront and useful only on bad days.

definition: The strike price, or exercise price, is the fixed level in an option contract at which the underlying may be bought, for a call, or sold, for a put. Exchanges list multiple strikes per expiry at prescribed intervals, and the relationship between the strike and the underlying market price determines the option's moneyness and intrinsic value. Whether a contract finishes in the money is judged by comparing the settlement price of the underlying with the strike.
plainEnglish: The predetermined price written into the option deal. Everything about the option revolves around whether the market price finishes above or below this line.

definition: The spot price is the current market price of the underlying asset for immediate settlement, as opposed to the futures price for a later date or the strike written into an option. In Indian derivative analysis it is usually taken as the underlying index level or stock price at the moment of evaluation. The gap between spot and futures prices is the basis, which converges toward zero as expiry approaches.
plainEnglish: Today's cash price of the thing the contract tracks, like the live Nifty level. Derivatives are judged against this number.

definition: The option premium is the price the buyer pays and the seller receives for an option contract, quoted per unit of the underlying and settled upfront under SEBI's framework, which requires the premium to be collected in full from option buyers. The premium decomposes into intrinsic value, reflecting how far the strike is from the underlying, and time value, reflecting the possibility of further favourable movement before expiry. Premiums are discovered continuously on the exchange and are influenced by volatility, time to expiry and rates.
plainEnglish: The fee for the choice an option gives you. Buyers pay it up front, and it is all they can lose; sellers pocket it and accept the obligation that follows.

definition: Intrinsic value is the amount by which an option is in the money, being the excess of the spot or settlement price of the underlying over the strike for a call, or the excess of the strike over the underlying for a put, and it is never negative for the buyer. Any premium beyond intrinsic value is time value, which decays as expiry approaches. At expiry, an option's value equals its intrinsic value, since no time remains for further movement.
plainEnglish: The part of an option's price that would be real profit if the contract expired right now. The rest is just hope for the future, which fades as expiry nears.

definition: Time value is the portion of an option premium in excess of intrinsic value, reflecting the probability that the option becomes more valuable before expiry. It is highest for at-the-money options and erodes as expiry approaches, reaching zero at expiry, a process known as time decay. Higher implied volatility raises time value because larger future moves are expected.
plainEnglish: The part of an option's price that is pure expectation about the future. Like ice in the sun, it melts steadily until expiry day, when only real value is left.

definition: Moneyness describes the position of an option's strike relative to the underlying market price, classifying the option as in the money, at the money or out of the money. It determines intrinsic value, and through it the option's delta, which measures how much the premium moves with the underlying. Moneyness is dynamic: an out-of-the-money option can become in the money if the underlying moves before expiry.
plainEnglish: Whether an option would pay off right now, is sitting exactly at break-even, or is currently worthless. That status changes every time the market moves.

definition: An option is in the money when exercising it at the current underlying price would yield a positive payoff: a call whose strike is below the underlying, or a put whose strike is above it. In-the-money options carry intrinsic value and typically higher premiums, and their deltas are larger in absolute magnitude than those of out-of-the-money options. As expiry approaches, time value on in-the-money options shrinks toward zero.
plainEnglish: An option that currently has real value: using it now would save or earn you money compared with the market price.

definition: An option is out of the money when exercising it at the current underlying price would produce no payoff: a call whose strike is above the underlying, or a put whose strike is below it. Such options consist entirely of time value, are cheaper than in-the-money options and have smaller deltas, but they offer leveraged exposure to a favourable move. Many option-selling strategies harvest the premiums of out-of-the-money contracts that expire worthless.
plainEnglish: An option that is currently worthless to use: the market must move further before it means anything. Cheap to buy, and the cheapest to lose everything on.

definition: An option is at the money when its strike is equal or very close to the current underlying price, giving it little or no intrinsic value but the highest time value of its series. At-the-money options have deltas near 0.5 in absolute terms and are the most sensitive to changes in implied volatility. They are the focus of straddle, strangle and delta-hedging strategies.
plainEnglish: The option sitting exactly at the current market price. It wins or loses on the smallest move in either direction, making it the most nerve-wracked contract in the chain.

definition: Delta measures the change in an option's premium for a one-unit change in the price of the underlying, representing both the option's price sensitivity and an approximation of the probability of finishing in the money for a call. Call deltas range from zero to one and put deltas from minus one to zero, with at-the-money values near 0.5 and minus 0.5 respectively. Market makers hedge by keeping their aggregate delta neutral, which channels option flows into the underlying market.
plainEnglish: How much an option's price will move when the asset moves by one rupee. A delta of 0.4 on a call means the option gains roughly 40 paise when the share rises a rupee.

definition: Gamma measures the rate of change of an option's delta for a one-unit change in the underlying price, capturing the curvature of the premium with respect to the underlying. Gamma is highest for at-the-money options near expiry and is what makes short-dated option positions unstable: deltas flip rapidly as the underlying moves. OptionSellers and hedgers watch gamma because it determines how often hedges must be adjusted to stay delta neutral.
plainEnglish: The next layer of sensitivity: how fast the option's sensitivity itself changes. High gamma means your hedge can become badly out of date the moment the market moves.

definition: Theta measures the change in an option's premium for the passage of one day, reflecting time decay, and is typically negative for long option positions, meaning the buyer loses premium value each day as expiry approaches. Theta accelerates as expiry nears for at-the-money options and is the structural income of option sellers. It gives options their reputation as wasting assets.
plainEnglish: The daily rent on holding an option: each morning the option is worth a little less simply because expiry is closer. Sellers collect this decay; buyers pay it.

definition: Vega measures the change in an option's premium for a change in implied volatility, all else equal, so a long option position gains when volatility expectations rise. Vega is largest for at-the-money options with longer time to expiry. It is the primary exposure through which traders take views on volatility rather than direction.
plainEnglish: How much the option's price jumps when the market starts expecting bigger swings. If fear rises, options with time left get more expensive.

definition: Rho measures the change in an option's premium for a change in the risk-free interest rate, with call values typically rising and put values falling when rates increase. It is the least influential of the standard sensitivities for short-dated options but becomes more relevant for long-dated contracts. In Indian markets it is rarely the focus of retail trading but appears in complete option-pricing frameworks.
plainEnglish: The effect of interest rates on an option's price. Small in day-to-day trading, noticeable only for options with months left to run.

definition: Implied volatility is the volatility input that makes a theoretical option-pricing model reproduce the observed market premium of an option, so it represents the market's consensus expectation of future volatility over the option's life. It is forward-looking, unlike historical volatility computed from past prices, and changes with supply, demand and event risk even when the underlying is static. Option-trading platforms in India quote IV per strike and expiry, and its pattern across strikes forms the volatility smile.
plainEnglish: The amount of price movement the options market is betting on, extracted backwards from option prices. Rising implied volatility means traders expect or fear bigger swings ahead.

definition: Historical volatility is the standard deviation of an asset's past returns over a chosen lookback window, annualised for comparability, giving a backward-looking measure of how much the asset actually moved. It serves as the baseline against which implied volatility is judged: when implied exceeds realised, options are relatively expensive, and when it falls short, premiums are relatively cheap. The estimate depends heavily on the lookback window and return frequency chosen.
plainEnglish: How much the market has actually been moving lately, measured from the record. Compare it with what options are pricing to judge whether protection is cheap or expensive.

definition: The volatility smile describes the pattern of implied volatilities across strike prices for a single expiry, typically higher for both deep out-of-the-money puts and calls than for at-the-money options, producing a U-shape; a persistent asymmetry toward puts, common in equity markets, is called skew. It exists because market participants price tail risk and supply-demand imbalances that a flat single-volatility model would ignore. The term structure of volatility compares implied volatilities across expiries, with short-dated options often pricing event risk.
plainEnglish: Option prices across the strike menu are not uniform: crash protection usually costs more than lottery tickets for the same distance, and that lopsided pattern is the smile or skew.

definition: Open interest is the number of derivative contracts that remain outstanding and unclosed at a point in time, increasing when new positions are created and decreasing when positions are offset or settled. Unlike trading volume, which counts activity during a session, open interest measures accumulated exposure and is often read alongside price to judge whether a move is being driven by new positioning. Indian exchanges publish contract-wise open interest daily, including participant-wise data.
plainEnglish: How many bets are still live on the table. Growing open interest means fresh money is entering; falling open interest means players are closing out.

definition: Lot size is the minimum quantity of the underlying covered by one derivative contract, fixed by the exchanges for each instrument under SEBI's framework, so that contract values stay above the minimum threshold the regulator prescribes. Because only whole lots can be traded, hedgers must round their required exposure to the nearest contract multiple, which creates basis and tracking mismatches. SEBI's 2024 measures for index derivatives raised minimum contract values, increasing the notional each lot represents.
plainEnglish: The fixed bundle size for a derivative contract: you buy contracts in whole bundles, not single shares. Bigger bundles mean bigger minimum bets.

fullName: Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk Margin
definition: SPAN margin is the initial margin computed by the exchange's portfolio-based risk system, which evaluates a position's worst-case loss under a set of simulated price and volatility scenarios and sets margin accordingly. It works at the level of the combined portfolio, so offsetting positions attract lower margin than the sum of their individual requirements. SEBI and the clearing corporations prescribe the framework within which SPAN operates in India, with margin collected from both buyers and sellers of futures and from option sellers.
plainEnglish: The security deposit the exchange makes you post, sized to how much your whole portfolio could plausibly lose in a bad scenario, so a hedged basket needs less than scattered bets.

definition: Exposure margin is an additional initial margin collected over and above SPAN margin in Indian derivatives markets, intended to cover risks arising from change in exposure and positions held beyond the scenario coverage of the SPAN framework. It is levied on the notional value of open positions as prescribed by the exchanges and clearing corporations. Together with SPAN margin and any additional or special margins the exchange prescribes, it forms the total initial margin locked for a derivative position.
plainEnglish: A top-up deposit added to the main risk deposit, covering the sort of market gaps the standard system does not imagine.

definition: Mark-to-market is the daily process in futures and short option positions by which the day's change in contract value is settled in cash between the parties, so profits and losses are realised continuously rather than at expiry. In India the clearing corporation debits and credits member and client accounts on a daily settlement cycle, meaning positions require funding well before final realisation. Failure to meet a mark-to-market obligation triggers margin calls and possible position closure.
plainEnglish: The daily squaring of the books: if your futures position gains ₹2,000 today, that money comes into your account today; if it loses, you must top up by tomorrow.

definition: Settlement is the process of closing out the obligations of a derivative contract, either through cash payment of the final difference between contract and settlement price or through delivery of the underlying, as the contract specifications require. Indian index derivatives are settled in cash at the expiry settlement price prescribed by the exchange, while stock derivatives move to physical delivery in the current framework. The clearing corporation guarantees settlement, standing between buyer and seller, which removes counterparty credit risk between members.
plainEnglish: The endgame of a contract: either cash changes hands for the final difference or the actual shares are delivered. The exchange's clearing house ensures both sides honour it.

definition: Physical settlement requires the seller of an in-the-money derivative position to deliver the underlying securities and the buyer to pay for them, rather than cash-settling the difference. In India it applies to single-stock futures and options that are held to expiry in the money, with delivery obligations passed through the clearing corporation to brokers and clients, funded by the full contract value rather than margin. Index derivatives, by contrast, are cash-settled because an index cannot be delivered.
plainEnglish: Finishing the contract by actually handing over the shares, not just paying the difference. If you sold a stock option that ended in the money, you must deliver the shares and receive the strike amount.

definition: Exercise is the action by which an option holder uses the right granted by the contract to buy, for a call, or sell, for a put, the underlying at the strike price. For cash-settled index options in India, exercise at expiry results in a cash payment equal to the intrinsic value rather than a securities transaction. On the seller's side, the corresponding obligation is termed assignment.
plainEnglish: Using your option: telling the exchange you want to act on your right to buy or sell at the agreed price. If it pays, holders exercise; if not, they let it lapse.

definition: Assignment is the process by which the seller of an option is designated, typically on a random or pro-rata basis among matched sellers, to fulfil the obligation when the buyer exercises. The assigned writer must deliver the underlying, for a call, or pay for it, for a put, according to the contract terms and settlement method. Assignment risk is the reason deep in-the-money American-style short options can be exercised and assigned ahead of expiry.
plainEnglish: The flip side of exercise: when someone uses the option you sold, the exchange taps you to honour the deal at the strike price.

definition: A European option can be exercised only at expiry, not at any earlier date, which simplifies valuation and trading mechanics and is the style used for exchange-traded index options in India. The value of a European option is driven by the distribution of the underlying at expiry alone. All the standard model-based Greeks and implied-volatility quotations are computed on European exercise.
plainEnglish: A contract where the choice can be used only on the finish line, at expiry, not midway. Indian index options work this way.

definition: An American option may be exercised at any time up to and including expiry, giving the holder timing flexibility that a European option lacks and, in principle, making it at least as valuable as its European counterpart. Early exercise has value mainly when the option is deep in the money or when the underlying pays dividends, because otherwise the time value forgone exceeds the benefit. Indian exchange-traded derivative contracts operate under the exercise styles prescribed in their contract specifications, with index options being European.
plainEnglish: A contract you can use any day you like until expiry, not just on the last day. More freedom for the holder, more uncertainty for the seller.

definition: A covered call position combines a long holding in the underlying with the sale of a call option on the same underlying, generating premium income at the cost of capping upside above the strike.
