It is used to enhance yield on stocks the investor is willing to sell at a target price, and the premium partially cushions downside moves. The strategy underperforms a plain holding if the underlying rallies sharply beyond the strike.
plainEnglish: Selling someone the right to buy your shares at a higher price and pocketing the fee. You earn extra cash now, but you have agreed to give away any big rally above that price.

definition: A protective put combines a long position in the underlying with the purchase of a put option on it, establishing a floor below which the position cannot lose during the option's life, in exchange for the premium paid. It functions as portfolio insurance, with the cost known in advance, and allows the investor to retain upside above the strike. Rebuying protection repeatedly makes the strategy costly over long periods, and strike selection trades insurance quality against premium outlay.
plainEnglish: Buying insurance for your shares: you pay a fee, and if the price crashes below your chosen level, the put pays you back while you keep any gains above it.

definition: A straddle combines the purchase or sale of a call and a put on the same underlying with the same strike and expiry, positioned at or near the money. The long straddle profits from large moves in either direction and pays for the double premium with high sensitivity to volatility, while the short straddle earns the two premiums and loses on large moves. Straddle performance is dominated by the realised volatility of the underlying relative to its implied volatility.
plainEnglish: Betting on turbulence, not direction: you buy both the up-option and the down-option at the same price. You win only if the market moves big, either way.

definition: A strangle pairs an out-of-the-money call with an out-of-the-money put of the same expiry, costing less than a straddle because both legs start with no intrinsic value but requiring a larger move to become profitable. A short strangle collects two premiums and profits from range-bound markets and time decay, at the risk of unbounded loss on a sharp move. It is the staple income strategy of option sellers in Indian index derivatives.
plainEnglish: A cheaper turbulence bet: you buy options that are both currently out of reach. The market must move a lot before you profit, but you pay less to get in.

definition: An iron condor is a defined-risk, range-bound options strategy combining a short strangle with protective long options at further-out strikes, so the maximum loss is capped while the maximum profit is the net premium received. It suits a view that the underlying will stay within a band until expiry and benefits from time decay. Because both the profit and the loss are capped, the payoff resembles selling insurance with a reinsurance cushion.
plainEnglish: Winning if the market just stays calm inside a range, with the built-in insurance that limits how badly you can lose if it does not.

definition: A calendar spread takes long and short positions in options of the same strike or nearby strikes but different expiries, seeking to profit from the different rates of time decay and changes in the volatility term structure across maturities. The position is sensitive to both implied volatility levels and the passage of time on each leg. Under SEBI's 2024 measures, the margin benefit previously available on calendar spreads in index derivatives was removed, making such structures costlier to hold.
plainEnglish: Trading one expiry date against another: sell the fast-melting option, hold the later one. The bet is on time and volatility, not just direction.

definition: Basis is the difference between the spot price of an underlying and its futures price for a given expiry, driving cash-and-carry arbitrage and hedging outcomes. In normal markets, futures trade above spot, reflecting carrying costs such as financing and storage; the basis converges to zero as expiry approaches because the two prices must coincide at settlement. For hedgers, an imperfect match between the contract used and the exposure being hedged leaves basis risk even when the hedge is otherwise effective.
plainEnglish: The gap between the price today and the price for later delivery. It shrinks to zero by expiry, and whoever hedges takes on the risk of that gap moving unpredictably.

definition: Contango describes a futures market in which prices for later delivery trade above the spot price, usually reflecting the cost of carrying the asset, such as interest, storage and insurance. Equity index futures in India frequently trade in contango because financing costs dominate, and the premium decays as expiry approaches, creating returns for buyers of the spot and sellers of futures. Persistent contango is the normal state of a well-functioning hedging market.
plainEnglish: When tomorrow's price is higher than today's, the market is in contango. Sell-side hedgers accept paying the premium for the certainty of a locked price.

definition: Backwardation describes a futures market in which later-dated contracts trade below the spot price, implying negative carry and signalling tightness or strong immediate demand for the underlying. In equity markets it can appear when borrowing is scarce or when dividends and expectations of price declines dominate the cost of carry, while in commodities it reflects convenience yield. Positioned holders can gain as the basis converges, but backwardation often signals stress rather than opportunity.
plainEnglish: The opposite of contango: tomorrow's price is below today's. It usually signals that people want the asset right now more than the promise of it later.

definition: India VIX is a volatility index computed by NSE from the prices of Nifty 50 index options using a model-independent methodology, and it expresses the market's expected annualised volatility of the index over roughly the next month. Rising values accompany fear and hedging demand, while compressed values mark complacency, so it is colloquially called the market's fear gauge. Because it is derived from option premiums rather than historical prices, it updates with market expectations in real time.
plainEnglish: A fear thermometer for the Nifty, read off option prices. When it spikes, investors are paying up for protection and expecting big swings.

fullName: Non-Banking Financial Company — Peer to Peer Lending Platform
definition: An NBFC-P2P is a company registered with the RBI under the master direction governing peer-to-peer lending platforms, which operates an online marketplace matching lenders with individual borrowers. The framework requires the platform to act only as an intermediary, forbids it from guaranteeing returns, promising liquidity, providing credit enhancement or lending on its own account, and prescribes exposure limits for lenders across borrowers and platforms. Platforms must maintain escrow arrangements for funds and comply with KYC, reporting and fair-practice norms.
plainEnglish: A licensed online matchmaker between people willing to lend money and people wanting to borrow it. It may not take sides, guarantee anything or hold your money directly.

definition: In peer-to-peer lending, the lender is the retail user who commits money through a registered platform to one or several borrowers in units of participating loans, bearing the credit risk directly. The RBI framework caps a lender's aggregate exposure to a single borrower and across all platforms at prescribed levels, precisely because the lender, not the platform, owns the default risk. Lenders receive interest and principal as repayments come in, with no promise of positive returns from the platform.
plainEnglish: The person putting up the money in a P2P deal. You are behaving like a mini bank, your money spreads across many borrowers, and if some do not repay, that loss is yours.

definition: In peer-to-peer lending, the borrower is the verified individual or eligible entity that receives a loan originated through the platform, with KYC and credit assessment conducted under the RBI-prescribed framework. Borrowers are typically seeking unsecured personal or small-business credit, often at rates that reflect weaker credit profiles than bank-grade lending. The platform must disclose the borrower's risk grade and loan terms, but the loan contract is between lender and borrower.
plainEnglish: The person on the other side looking for a loan. Often they come to a P2P platform because banks will not lend to them, which is exactly why the interest can be tempting and the risk real.

definition: The platform fee is the charge a peer-to-peer lending platform levies for matching services, typically deducted from repayments received or charged to borrowers when a loan is funded, and disclosed in the platform's terms. It is separate from servicing charges and from any charges embedded in the loan's interest rate, and it directly reduces the lender's net yield. Because platforms cannot guarantee returns, all fees must be transparently disclosed under the RBI framework.
plainEnglish: The matchmaker's commission, taken whether or not the loan gets repaid. It is why a flashy gross interest rate shrinks once you subtract the platform bites.

definition: A servicing fee is the recurring charge deducted from collections for administering a peer-to-peer loan, covering repayment processing, reminders, collection coordination and reporting to the lender. It is distinct from the one-time platform matching fee and from any penal interest charged to defaulting borrowers. Net returns to lenders are calculated after both fees, so quoted gross rates overstate realised yields.
plainEnglish: The ongoing maintenance charge for keeping your loan on the books, taken out of each repayment as it comes in.

definition: A risk grade is a platform-assigned classification of a borrower's creditworthiness, derived from bureau data, income, employment stability and loan purpose, used to set the interest rate offered and to give lenders a comparative risk indicator. Grades are typically expressed as alphanumeric tiers with associated historical performance statistics, but they are the platform's internal opinion, not a regulated rating. Lenders should track whether realised losses in each grade match the advertised expectations.
plainEnglish: A letter grade stamped on the borrower, like a school report: A-grade borrowers are expected to repay nearly always, lower grades less so but at higher interest. The grade is the platform's judgement, not a guarantee.

definition: Vintage refers to the month or quarter in which a set of loans was originated, enabling performance comparison across cohorts at the same age since disbursal. Vintage analysis reveals whether a platform's underwriting is improving or deteriorating, because newer cohorts have had less time to season and defaults emerge mainly in the early months of a loan's life. It is the standard lens for judging a lending book honestly.
plainEnglish: Grouping loans by when they were issued, like wines by year, so you can compare them fairly at the same age and see if the newer ones are behaving better or worse.

definition: Delinquency is the state of a loan on which a scheduled payment has been missed but the obligation has not been written off, typically categorised by how many days the payment is overdue. Delinquency rates are the leading indicator of credit deterioration in a peer-to-peer portfolio and generally worsen with the age of the book as loans season. The boundary between delinquency and formal default is defined by the classification norms applied to the pool.
plainEnglish: A loan that has started missing payments but is not yet given up on. The longer it stays delinquent, the less likely the money comes back.

definition: Days past due counts the number of days by which a scheduled loan payment is overdue as of the reporting date, and it is the standard unit for bucketing delinquent loans, such as 1-30, 31-90 and 90-plus days. Regulatory asset-classification norms in India use DPD thresholds to define non-performing status for lenders, and counting conventions matter because a single missed EMI moves a loan through the buckets. DPD roll rates, showing the proportion of loans moving from one bucket to the next, are a key behavioural indicator.
plainEnglish: How late a payment is, measured in days. There is a big difference between someone paying three days late and someone three months behind, and lenders track the buckets carefully.

definition: Default is the failure to meet a contractual debt obligation when due, ranging from a borrower who has stopped servicing the loan to an issuer missing an interest payment or redemption, and it is what probability of default and loss given default models estimate in advance. In the retail-lending context, classification as a non-performing asset follows the prescribed DPD-based norms, though recovery efforts may continue long after. A default is not the same as a write-off: the loan may be classified and later partially recovered.
plainEnglish: The borrower has genuinely stopped paying, not just run a few days late. The lender books it as a problem asset but may still chase the money.

definition: Recovery is the money actually collected on a defaulted or written-off loan after normal servicing has failed, through collections pressure, legal action, settlement or sale of the platform's rights. In peer-to-peer portfolios, recovery performance varies substantially by borrower segment and by the platform's collection infrastructure, and returned amounts are shared among lenders in proportion to their exposure. The recovery rate on a defaulted book determines the difference between the headline default rate and the realised loss.
plainEnglish: The money clawed back after things go bad. Some defaulted borrowers eventually pay something, some pay nothing, and recovery measures what actually lands in lenders' accounts.

definition: A write-off is the accounting recognition that a loan is unlikely to be recovered in full, removing it from the active book even though collection efforts may continue. For lenders in a peer-to-peer portfolio, a written-off amount usually represents a permanent capital loss unless a later recovery, which is credited back, materialises. Write-off timing policies differ across platforms, which makes comparing headline loss rates across platforms misleading.
plainEnglish: The moment the lender stops pretending and books the loss. The debt may still be chased, but your account statement has already marked it down.

definition: Collections refers both to the money received from borrowers against scheduled and overdue repayments and to the discipline of pursuing it, comprising reminders, call-centre follow-up, field collection and legal escalation as accounts age. The efficiency of a lender's or platform's collection engine drives the roll rate from delinquency to default and the eventual recovery rate. Collection practices are subject to fair-practice and conduct requirements under the RBI framework.
plainEnglish: The chasing department: reminding borrowers, following up on missed payments, and recovering as much as possible, politely but persistently.

definition: Principal loss is the portion of the original loan amount that a lender never recovers after a borrower defaults, arising when recoveries fall short of the outstanding principal before considering accrued interest. In unsecured peer-to-peer lending, principal losses can be large and are the reason diversification across many small exposures is emphasised. The expected principal loss on a pool is the product of default rate and loss given default applied to the aggregate exposure.
plainEnglish: The part of your original money that is simply gone. Interest earned elsewhere has to cover these holes before you are actually ahead.

definition: Accrued interest in retail lending is the interest that has been earned on a loan but not yet received in cash, recorded on an accrual basis. In distressed pools, accrued interest on defaulted exposures is frequently written back, so portfolio reports that count accrued interest at face value can overstate true recoveries. Distinguishing cash interest received from accrued interest is essential for honest return measurement.
plainEnglish: Interest that has piled up on the ledger but has not actually arrived in your account. If the borrower is not paying, interest that keeps accruing is paper money.

definition: Cash-flow IRR is the internal rate of return computed from the actual dated cash flows of a lending portfolio, incorporating disbursements, repayments, fees and recoveries, so it reflects the true money-weighted outcome of the investment. It differs from advertised yields, which often assume no defaults and no idle cash, and it captures the drag of reinvestment delays. For peer-to-peer lenders, comparing the cash-flow IRR against the platform headline is the honest test of realised performance.
plainEnglish: The actual annual return on your lending money, computed from every rupee that went out and came back and when. It is the only number that matters, once defaults and fees are included.

definition: Concentration risk is the danger of outsized losses from exposure to a single borrower, sector, platform or region, rather than from the average behaviour of a diversified pool. RBI's peer-to-peer framework addresses it with lender-level exposure caps per borrower and per platform, and portfolio practice extends the principle to granular loan sizes and diversified risk grades. Diversification reduces idiosyncratic loss variability but cannot eliminate the systematic credit cycle.
plainEnglish: Putting too much of your money on one borrower or one platform. If that single bet fails, the average is irrelevant, you lose a chunk outright.

definition: An escrow account is a designated bank account, operated under an arrangement permitted by the RBI framework, through which borrower repayments are collected and distributed to lenders by a peer-to-peer platform, keeping platform funds separate from investor funds. The escrow structure mitigates commingling risk and supports orderly settlement of collections, refunds and fees. Lenders should understand whether funds flow through the platform's escrow or a scheduled-bank-backed arrangement and how delays are handled.
plainEnglish: A neutral holding account where your repayments sit briefly before reaching you, so the platform cannot mix your money with its own.

definition: Auto-invest is a peer-to-peer platform feature that automatically allocates incoming money across eligible loans according to lender-set criteria such as risk grade, tenor and borrower profile, enabling rapid diversification without manual selection. It improves operational efficiency but can mask the quality of the underlying underwriting, because the lender may not examine individual loans. Lenders should review auto-invest outputs against realised vintage performance before allowing it to run at scale.
plainEnglish: A robot that spreads your money across many loans the moment it arrives, following settings you choose. Handy for diversification, but do not let it hide what you actually own.

definition: Borrower concentration measures the share of a lender's or platform's book exposed to a single borrower, expressed for an individual as the exposure versus total capital committed, and for a platform as the largest borrower exposures versus total originations. The RBI framework prescribes limits on a lender's exposure to a single borrower, and disciplined lending keeps individual ticket sizes small relative to the portfolio. High borrower concentration converts a diversified statistical bet into a handful of binary outcomes.
plainEnglish: How much of your lending money rides on any one person. Ten loans of ₹1,000 each is a portfolio; one loan of ₹10,000 is a gamble.

definition: Asset allocation is the division of a portfolio among broad asset classes such as equity, debt, gold, real estate and cash, which determines most of the portfolio's return level and volatility over long periods. Strategic choices about these proportions are made in light of goals, time horizon, risk capacity and valuation, and they precede security selection in importance. In Indian practice, allocation is frequently expressed as a debt-equity split adjusted with smaller gold and international components.
plainEnglish: How you divide your money between the big buckets: shares, bonds, gold, cash. Getting these proportions right matters more than picking the perfect stock.

definition: Strategic asset allocation is the long-term target mix of asset classes set from the investor's goals, horizon, risk capacity and capital-market assumptions, and it serves as the policy portfolio against which tactical bets are measured. It is typically documented in an investment policy statement and changed only for structural reasons such as a shift in goal horizon or a major change in circumstances. Rebalancing keeps the actual portfolio aligned with the strategic targets.
plainEnglish: Your permanent plan for how money is divided between asset types, written down and revisited rarely. It is the map; day-to-day decisions are just the driving.

definition: Tactical asset allocation is the deliberate short- to medium-term deviation of portfolio weights from strategic targets to exploit perceived relative value, momentum or macro conditions, usually within pre-set bands. It is distinct from stock selection and from strategic policy, and its success depends on the quality of the signal and the discipline of the bands. Without tight rules, tactical moves degenerate into performance chasing, which is why many advisers limit them to modest deviations.
plainEnglish: Small, temporary tilts away from your long-term plan, like leaning forward on a bus when you think it will stop soon. Useful only if you are honest about when you were wrong.

definition: Rebalancing is the periodic realignment of portfolio weights back to their targets after market movements have shifted them, done by selling overweighted assets and buying underweighted ones or by directing fresh flows to lagging sleeves. It enforces a contrarian discipline: trimming what has run up and adding to what has fallen, and it controls risk drift over time. Rebalancing may be calendar-based, threshold-based or a combination, and tax and transaction costs are deducted from the benefit in taxable accounts.
plainEnglish: Resetting your mix when the market has shifted it: sell some of whatever has ballooned, add to whatever has shrunk, back to plan. It makes you buy low and sell high, mechanically.

definition: Risk parity allocates capital so that each asset class contributes equal risk, measured by volatility or contribution to portfolio variance, rather than equal money; lower-volatility assets such as bonds therefore receive larger weights. The approach requires leverage or careful constraints when applied to return-seeking portfolios, and its long-run behaviour depends on the stability of volatility and correlation estimates. In India it is discussed in the context of multi-asset funds and PMS mandates rather than pure retail implementation.
plainEnglish: Instead of splitting money equally, split the worry equally: gentle assets get more money so each part of the portfolio contributes the same amount of bumpiness.

definition: Mean-variance optimisation, introduced by Harry Markowitz, computes portfolio weights that maximise expected return for a given level of variance, or minimise variance for a given return, using inputs of expected returns, volatilities and correlations. Its output is highly sensitive to estimation error in the inputs, particularly expected returns, so naive use produces unstable, concentrated allocations. Practical implementations add constraints, resampling or shrinkage and are compared against simple rule-based portfolios.
plainEnglish: A mathematical recipe for the best trade-off between average return and wobbliness. Powerful on paper, famously easy to fool with wrong estimates of the future.

definition: The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios offering the highest expected return for each level of risk, or equivalently the lowest risk for each expected return, in the mean-variance framework. Portfolios below the frontier are dominated because a better combination of risk and return is available. The frontier shifts with changes in the inputs and does not incorporate borrowing constraints, taxes or liquidity, so it is a conceptual tool rather than an operational answer.
plainEnglish: The boundary line of the best possible trade-offs between return and bumpiness: everything on the line is efficient, everything below it is a worse deal.

definition: The capital allocation line shows combinations of the risk-free asset and a risky portfolio, tracing how expected return rises linearly with risk as more capital is shifted into the risky portfolio. Its slope is the Sharpe ratio of the risky portfolio, so the steepest available line identifies the most efficient risky combination. The line structure formalises the choice of how much risk to take, given an efficient mix of risky assets.
plainEnglish: A straight line from the bank deposit to the best risky basket, showing every blend of the two. The steeper the line, the better the basket rewards risk.

definition: The tangency portfolio is the risky portfolio at the point where the capital allocation line touches the efficient frontier, the mix with the highest Sharpe ratio among all feasible risky combinations when a risk-free asset is available. Investors combine it with lending or borrowing at the risk-free rate to reach their preferred risk level. Its composition is extremely sensitive to input estimates, which is why practical allocations regularise it or constrain the weights.
plainEnglish: The single best risky basket, the one that gives the most reward per unit of wobble. Mix it with bank deposits to dial your risk up or down.

definition: The Black-Litterman model blends the market-implied equilibrium returns from a mean-variance framework with an investor's specific views and confidence levels, producing posterior expected returns that are more stable than raw historical estimates. Portfolio weights derived from these posteriors deviate from the market portfolio only in proportion to stated conviction, mitigating the extreme allocations of unconstrained optimisation. It is used in institutional allocation and multi-asset mandates.
plainEnglish: A way to mix the market's overall opinion with your own view politely: modest tilts where you are confident, no wild bets where you are not.

definition: A glide path is a pre-scheduled shift in asset allocation over an investor's life or a goal's horizon, conventionally from higher equity exposure when the horizon is long and the corpus small to a more defensive mix as the target date approaches. It reduces sequence risk near the goal date, when a market fall would be hardest to recover from, and it is embedded in target-date-style products and NPS lifecycle options. The slope and endpoint of the path are design choices driven by the saver's risk capacity and contribution pattern.
plainEnglish: A planned landing: start with a share-heavy portfolio when retirement is far away, then gradually add safety as the date comes closer, like a plane letting down slowly.

definition: Sequence-of-returns risk is the danger that the order in which returns arrive, rather than their average, determines whether a withdrawal plan survives, because early losses combined with ongoing withdrawals permanently impair the corpus. Two investors with identical average returns can have radically different outcomes if one experiences bad years early in the drawdown phase. Strategies to manage it include bucket allocations, lower initial withdrawal rates and flexibility to reduce spending after bad years.
plainEnglish: Withdrawing money during a crash hurts much more than the same crash while you are still saving, because the money you take out never gets the recovery. Timing of bad luck matters as much as its size.

definition: A safe withdrawal rate is the initial percentage of a retirement corpus that can be withdrawn annually, with subsequent increases for inflation, while keeping the probability of corpus depletion within an acceptable bound in historical or simulated scenarios. Classic research arrived at low-single-digit rates for long retirements, and Indian conditions, higher inflation and different asset returns alter the appropriate figure. The rate is a planning heuristic, not a guarantee, and should be paired with review points and spending flexibility.
plainEnglish: The share of your nest egg you can safely spend each year without running out: commonly discussed as roughly 3-4%, though India's inflation makes it a moving target.

definition: A bucket strategy divides a retirement corpus into layered buckets by time horizon: near-term spending needs held in cash and short-duration debt, medium-term needs in conservative balanced assets and long-term growth capital in equity. Withdrawals are drawn first from the near bucket, which is replenished when markets are favourable, making the strategy a practical answer to sequence-of-returns risk. It trades some theoretical return for behavioural comfort and clearer operational rules.
plainEnglish: Three labelled jars of money: one for the next two years of spending, one for after that, and one left to grow. You spend from the nearest jar so a market crash does not force you to sell shares at the bottom.

definition: Correlation breakdown is the tendency of correlations between asset classes to rise toward one during periods of market stress, including correlations that are normally low or negative, destroying the diversification benefit precisely when it is needed. It arises from common liquidity and deleveraging shocks that force sales across portfolios simultaneously. The lesson is to stress-test diversification using crisis-window correlations rather than relying solely on long-run averages.
plainEnglish: All your supposedly independent investments falling together in a crash. Diversification works on ordinary days; on disaster days everything drops at once, which is exactly when you notice.

definition: Home bias is the tendency of investors to allocate a disproportionate share of their portfolios to domestic assets despite the global opportunity set, driven by familiarity, currency comfort, tax friction and regulatory frictions such as remittance limits. Indian investors exhibit strong home bias, holding portfolios heavily weighted to domestic equity and property. The cost of home bias is reduced diversification and concentrated exposure to a single country's policy, inflation and currency.
plainEnglish: Putting almost everything in your own country's markets because they feel safe and familiar, even though the world is bigger. It shrinks your options and concentrates your risks.

definition: Rental yield is the annual rent received from a property divided by its capital value or purchase price, expressing the income return on a property investment before costs. Gross yield uses rent before expenses while net yield deducts maintenance, property tax, vacancy and management costs, and Indian residential yields are typically lower than commercial yields. It should be compared against the risk-free rate and the property's carrying costs to judge the income case for owning rather than renting.
plainEnglish: The yearly rent as a percentage of what the property costs: a ₹1 crore flat rented at ₹2.5 lakh a year yields 2.5%. Often less than a bank deposit, before costs.

definition: The capitalisation rate is a property's net operating income divided by its current market value, used to value income-producing real estate by capitalising the income stream. It is inversely related to price: as cap rates compress, values rise for the same rental income, and widening cap rates signal repricing. In Indian commercial real estate, cap rates for grade-A assets are watched as a key valuation gauge, and the same measure underpins REIT income yields.
plainEnglish: The property world's version of an interest rate: annual net rent divided by price. A 7% cap rate on ₹1 crore of rent implies a value of about ₹14 crore.

definition: Under RERA, carpet area is the net usable floor area of an apartment excluding the external walls, area under services shafts and the exclusive balcony and verandah area, though it includes the internal partition walls, as specified in the Act. Developers must disclose carpet area for each apartment as the basis for sale and for the computation of any area-based refund or penalty. Because marketing frequently quotes built-up or super built-up area, comparing price per carpet-area square foot is the only like-for-like test of what a buyer is paying for.
plainEnglish: The floor space you can actually walk on inside the flat, excluding the thick walls and shared areas. It is the honest square-footage number the law requires builders to reveal.

definition: Built-up area is the carpet area plus the thickness of external and internal walls, and in common market practice also includes the balcony area as defined by the developer. It is larger than carpet area by the wall thickness component, and none of the components are standardised across projects the way carpet area is under RERA. Buyers comparing projects should use carpet area and the disclosed price basis to avoid confusion.
plainEnglish: The flat plus its walls, roughly 10-15% more floor space than the carpet area you can actually use. A bigger-sounding number for the same flat.

definition: Super built-up area is the built-up area of an apartment plus its proportionate share of common areas such as lobbies, staircases, lifts, corridors and amenity space, sometimes called the saleable area. The loading factor, the ratio of super built-up to carpet or built-up area, varies by project and is a negotiating as well as a disclosure matter. Price per super built-up square foot can look low while the effective usable-space cost is high.
plainEnglish: The flat plus the walls plus a share of the building's corridors and common spaces. The number advertised in brochures, and the one you should trust least.

definition: Stamp duty is a state-level tax on the transfer of immovable property, calculated on the higher of the consideration or the minimum value determined under state law, and collected at the time of registration. Rates, exemptions and concessional schemes vary by state and are revised in state budgets, so the duty on the same transaction differs across India. An unstamped or under-stamped instrument can be inadmissible as evidence and attracts penalties, making duty computation central to any property transaction.
plainEnglish: The state government's cut on any property sale, usually a percentage of the price, paid when you register the purchase. Plus registration fees on top.

definition: A circle rate is the minimum per-square-metre or per-square-foot value of land and buildings notified by state revenue authorities for a locality, used as the floor for stamp-duty computation, with registration of transactions below it generally barred or permitted only with higher authorities' approval on evidence of genuine distress prices. When the actual consideration is below the circle rate, the difference can attract tax consequences under the deeming provisions of the Income-tax Act. Circle rates are revised periodically and vary by locality and property type.
plainEnglish: A government rate card for property values by locality. Even if you strike a cheaper deal privately, the stamp duty and tax machinery may insist on the official minimum value.

definition: RERA establishes the framework for regulation and development of the real estate sector, requiring promoters to register projects above the prescribed size before advertising or selling, disclose project approvals, timelines and sanctioned plans, and deposit a mandated share of collections in a designated account to be drawn down in proportion to construction progress. It creates state real-estate regulatory authorities with powers of adjudication and penalties, and defines the rights of allottees including remedies for delayed possession. Carpet-area definition, sale-contract standardisation and interest-rate penal provisions for defaults flow from the Act.
plainEnglish: India's real-estate rulebook: builders must register projects, stick to disclosed timelines, keep buyers' money in escrow and face penalties for delays. It gives homebuyers a formal forum to complain.

definition: Redevelopment is the demolition and reconstruction of an old property or society building, usually on land owned collectively by existing members, with the developer funding construction in exchange for additional saleable area and the members receiving new or larger flats. In Mumbai and other dense cities, the process runs through society resolutions, development agreements, and RERA obligations on the new project, and it is governed by the transfer-of-development-rights rules of the state. Members should weigh corpus offers, rent compensation during construction and quality guarantees alongside the headline area gain.
plainEnglish: Tearing down an old building and putting up a new one, with a developer funding it in return for extra floors to sell. Existing flat owners get new flats, sometimes bigger, plus rent while they wait.

definition: A joint development agreement is a contract between a landowner and a developer under which the landowner contributes land and the developer funds and executes construction, with the consideration structured as a share of constructed area, cash, or a combination. The agreement allocates approvals, timelines, marketing rights, penalties and exit rights, and its tax treatment for the landowner upon transfer of rights has been clarified by tax rulings and provisions on capital gains and construction advances. Unregistered or loosely drafted JDAs are a recurring source of litigation.
plainEnglish: The landowner brings the plot, the builder brings the money and skill, and they split the built property in agreed proportions. Everything depends on how well the written contract covers delays and defaults.

definition: The loan-to-value ratio is the loan amount divided by the appraised value of the property, determining the down payment required and the lender's cushion against price decline. Indian lenders generally fund a proportion of the property's value subject to RBI and internal norms, with higher LTVs charged higher rates or sought with additional security. A higher LTV benefits the borrower with lower upfront cash but increases the loan cost and the risk of negative equity if prices fall.
plainEnglish: What share of the property price the bank is willing to lend: an 80% LTV on a ₹50 lakh flat means a ₹10 lakh down payment and a ₹40 lakh loan.

definition: An encumbrance certificate is a register extract issued by the property registration authority showing registered transactions on a property over a given period, revealing mortgages, liens, agreements and prior transfers. It is a standard component of property due diligence in India, though it only records registered encumbrances and cannot capture unregistered claims. It should be read together with title documents, municipal records and a physical survey before any purchase.
plainEnglish: A government certificate listing everything officially recorded against a property: loans taken on it, old sales, legal charges. Not a full guarantee, but the first thing a lawyer checks.

definition: Sovereign gold bonds are government securities denominated in grams of gold, issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India in occasional tranches, with a fixed rate of interest paid semi-annually in addition to redemption value linked to the price of gold at maturity. They carry the sovereign's credit quality and avoid the storage and purity risks of physical gold, and their redemption terms and any exemptions on maturity gains are as specified in the issue terms and tax law. Tranches are issued periodically and the secondary-market availability of any specific tranche must be checked with the exchanges rather than assumed.
plainEnglish: A government IOU written in grams of gold: you get interest while you hold it and the gold price when it matures, without a locker or purity worries.

definition: A gold exchange traded fund is mutual fund scheme whose units are listed on the exchanges and whose NAV tracks the domestic price of physical gold, achieved by holding gold or gold-related instruments as permitted under SEBI's regulations. Investors get exchange liquidity and no vaulting costs or purity risk, at the cost of annual expenses and, for some products, custody and insurance charges. Price discovery in the ETF can deviate modestly from the underlying gold price, and investors should compare tracking difference across products.
plainEnglish: Gold held inside a mutual fund you trade on the stock exchange, like a share. Its price follows the metal, and you never see a coin or a locker.

definition: A gold savings fund is a fund-of-funds that invests predominantly in the units of a gold ETF, allowing systematic investments without a demat account, at the cost of a second layer of expenses relative to buying the ETF directly. It provides gold-price participation through an open-ended mutual fund structure, and its returns track the underlying ETF net of both levels of cost. It is a convenience product for investors who value SIP capability over minimal cost.
plainEnglish: A mutual fund wrapper around a gold ETF, so you can SIP into it without a trading account. You pay a tiny extra layer of fees for the convenience.

definition: Digital gold is a commercial arrangement under which a retailer or app sells fractional gold that is held in vaults by a partner bullion or vaulting company, with buy and sell prices set by the seller and no market-wide price discovery. It is not a SEBI-regulated security, does not typically carry a periodic independent valuation disclosure, and its exit price and liquidity are a function of the seller's terms rather than an exchange. Investors should read the vaulting, insurance and redemption conditions before treating it as an investment rather than a purchase of the metal.
plainEnglish: Gold you buy through an app, stored in someone's vault on your behalf. Convenient, but the seller decides the price and the exit terms, and no regulator stands behind the promise.

definition: The gold monetisation scheme allows households to deposit eligible gold with participating banks in short, medium or long-term tenures, receiving interest denominated in gold on the deposit and redemption in gold or cash, with the objective of mobilising idle household gold into productive use. Deposits are assayed upon deposit and accrue interest as specified in the scheme terms, and depositors must assess the liquidity constraints of the chosen tenure. The scheme is administered under Government of India and RBI guidelines and its terms have been revised over time.
plainEnglish: Lending your household gold to a bank to earn interest in grams instead of keeping it in a locker. You get it back, usually in metal, after the agreed term.

definition: Gold futures are standardised exchange-traded contracts for delivery of gold at a future date, trading on India's commodity derivatives exchanges under SEBI's regulatory framework, with prices linked to international gold and the rupee exchange rate. They are used by jewellers and importers to hedge price risk and by others to take directional positions, with margin and daily settlement mechanics as for other futures. Physical delivery obligations and the contract's delivery centres attach when positions are held to expiry.
plainEnglish: A locked-in price for gold delivered later, traded on an exchange. Jewellers use it to order their gold safely; traders use it to bet on the metal without touching it.

definition: The gold-silver ratio is the number of ounces of silver it takes to buy one ounce of gold, an indicator of the relative valuation of the two metals. Above its long-run average, silver looks cheap relative to gold; below, expensive, and ratio traders treat its extremes as signals. The ratio moves with industrial demand for silver, monetary demand for gold, real interest rates and dollar strength, and it is not a fixed law of nature.
plainEnglish: How many silver coins buy one gold coin. When the number is unusually high, silver is the cheaper relative bet, and vice versa.

fullName: Customs Duty on Gold and Silver
definition: Gold and silver imports attract customs duty, including any applicable cess, as prescribed by the central government from time to time, which drives a wedge between international and domestic prices. The duty level is a key input to jewellers' pricing, smuggling incentives and the local premium or discount on the metal, and it is adjusted in the Budget and by notification. Domestic futures and ETF prices embed this duty, so they do not track international quotes rupee-for-rupee.
plainEnglish: The tax the government charges when gold enters the country. It is the main reason Indian gold prices are higher than the same gold quoted abroad.

definition: Making charges are the jeweller's fabrication fee for converting bullion into jewellery, quoted either as a lump sum per gram or as a percentage of the metal value, and they vary with design complexity and retailer. They are typically non-recoverable on sale and are excluded from the resale price of jewellery, which is usually based on the prevailing metal rate with deductions for purity loss. The share of making charges plus GST in the total cost is why jewellery is a poor vehicle for short-term gold-price exposure.
plainEnglish: The labour fee a jeweller adds for turning plain gold into an ornament. You pay it on purchase but never get it back when you sell, so it eats into gold's gain.

definition: Physical gold is coin, bar or jewellery holdings, carrying complete purity, storage and resale frictions: assay costs, locker fees, insurance, the risk of undercarat or imitation pieces, and buy-sell spreads imposed by dealers. Resale of jewellery involves melting and purity deductions, while bars and coins trade at closer to the quoted price through organised channels. For investment exposure, the physical form is best considered for sums that genuinely require tangible, off-system holding.
plainEnglish: Gold you can hold: coins, bars, ornaments. Real and reassuring, but you pay for storage, insurance and purity checks, and selling usually means a haircut.

definition: Silver is both a precious and an industrial metal, whose price is driven by investment demand plus industrial consumption in solar, electronics and electrical applications, making it more cyclical and more volatile than gold. Indian investors access silver through physical holdings, exchange-traded products and commodity derivatives, and the metal's GST and duty structure affects the domestic price versus international parity. Its smaller market capitalisation than gold means larger percentage swings for the same flow of money.
plainEnglish: The other precious metal: half jewellery, half industrial raw material. Cheaper than gold and jumpier, moving twice as hard when sentiment shifts.

definition: A REIT is a SEBI-regulated trust that owns and operates income-producing real estate, often commercial offices or retail assets, and issues units that are listed on the stock exchanges, giving investors fractional ownership of large properties with professional management. The REIT regulations require a minimum asset base for registration, mandate distribution of at least 90% of net distributable cash flows to unit holders and prescribe borrowing limits and valuation cycles. Unit holders receive the distributions declared in proportion to their holding, and unit prices move with rents, asset values, interest rates and market sentiment.
plainEnglish: The listed landlord: it pools investor money to own big commercial buildings and passes the rents to unit holders. You get real-estate income without buying a building yourself.

definition: An infrastructure investment trust is a SEBI-regulated pooling vehicle that owns operating infrastructure assets such as toll roads, power transmission lines, gas pipelines and renewable projects, issuing listed units that entitle holders to distributions from the assets' cash flows. The InvIT regulations prescribe eligible asset categories, minimum asset size and unit-holder thresholds, distribution requirements and leverage limits, and the trust operates through a manager and trustee structure. Cash flows are typically contracted or concession-based, making the trust's income profile different from that of a REIT, with consequent exposure to traffic, tariff and counterparty risk.
plainEnglish: A listed trust that owns finished infrastructure projects like highways and earns the tolls, sending the money to investors as regular payouts.

definition: Net distributable cash flows are the cash flows of a REIT or InvIT available for distribution to unit holders after operational expenses, interest and debt service, capital expenditure on a maintenance basis and any mandatory reserves, computed as prescribed in the SEBI regulations and trust documents. At least 90% of NDCF must be distributed, and the trust discloses NDCF at least once every six months. Because NDCF is a cash measure rather than an accounting-profit measure, it can differ from reported net profit, especially where depreciation or fair-value changes are large.
plainEnglish: The rent and toll money actually left over after keeping the buildings running and servicing loans. That leftover, not the accounting profit, is what gets paid out to unit holders.

definition: Distribution per unit is the cash amount distributed to each REIT or InvIT unit for a defined period, usually disclosed quarterly and aggregated annually, and typically split into interest, dividend and return-of-capital components. Comparing DPU across periods is meaningful only relative to the issue price, the unit price and the payout frequency, and the composition of the distribution affects its tax treatment in the unit holder's hands. A declining DPU trend often signals asset-level stress or dilution from fresh unit issuance.
plainEnglish: The cash each unit of the trust earned you in the period, like a dividend per share. Check what it is made of, because the taxman treats interest, dividend and capital differently.

definition: The sponsor of a REIT or InvIT is the entity that settles the trust, contributes the initial assets and is subject to minimum unitholding requirements prescribed by SEBI, ensuring meaningful skin in the game. Sponsors typically include developers, infrastructure companies or financial institutions with a track record in the relevant asset class. The sponsor's identity matters because its ongoing relationship with the trust affects pipeline assets, conflicts of interest and alignment of incentives.
plainEnglish: The founding owner that hands its buildings or highways to the trust and must keep a slice of the units, so it shares the same ride as other investors.

definition: The manager of a REIT or InvIT is the SEBI-registered entity responsible for day-to-day operations, asset acquisition and disposal recommendations, leasing, financing and disclosures, acting under the oversight of the trustee and within the regulations. It earns management fees as disclosed in the trust documents and must meet eligibility and experience criteria. The manager's capability, fee structure and conflicts with the sponsor or its affiliates are central to evaluating the trust's governance.
plainEnglish: The management company actually running the trust: collecting rents, negotiating leases, buying new assets. It gets paid a fee for the job.

definition: The trustee of a REIT or InvIT is a SEBI-registered debenture trustee that holds the trust's assets for the benefit of unit holders and monitors compliance by the manager with the regulations, the trust deed and the offer documents. It must act in the interest of unit holders, address conflicts and approve related-party transactions within the regulatory framework. The separation of trustee from manager is the core investor-protection mechanism of the structure.
plainEnglish: The independent guardian of the trust's assets, making sure the managers follow the rules and that the buildings belong to the investors, not the staff.

definition: Weighted average lease expiry measures the average remaining term of a property portfolio's leases, weighted by the rent or leasable area each lease represents, and indicates the durability of the rental income. A long WALE with staggered expiries provides visible cash flow, while a short WALE concentrates re-leasing risk and repricing exposure in the near term. It should be read with the tenant-credit composition and the distribution of expiry years, because a portfolio can have a healthy average while facing a single-year cliff.
plainEnglish: How many years, on average, the current tenants are locked in to paying rent. Long is comforting; a big chunk expiring together is a red flag.

definition: Occupancy rate is the proportion of a property or portfolio's leasable area that is currently leased and income-producing, disclosed by REITs and commercial landlords as a core operating metric. It interacts with rents: falling occupancy typically forces rental concessions, while full occupancy supports rent escalation. For REIT analysis, occupancy should be examined together with the spread between in-place and market rents, since a fully leased asset might still be under-rented.
plainEnglish: How much of the building is actually filled with paying tenants. Empty floors earn nothing and pull the payout down.

definition: Yield on cost is an asset's net operating income divided by the total cost a trust paid to acquire or develop it, showing the return the trust earns on its original investment rather than on the asset's current market value. As market rents rise, an older acquisition's yield on cost increases even if its cap rate at current values is unchanged, demonstrating the value of buying well. The metric is useful for judging a manager's acquisition discipline but is not directly comparable across trusts with different purchase vintages.
plainEnglish: The rent cheque measured against the price the trust originally paid for the building, not its value today. A high number means they bought well or rents have since risen.

definition: SEBI's REIT and InvIT regulations require distribution of at least 90% of net distributable cash flows to unit holders, with payouts made no less frequently than the prescribed intervals and disclosed under the trust's reporting obligations. The requirement is designed to make these vehicles structured income products rather than growth vehicles and prevents indefinite accumulation of cash inside the trust. The balance retained, together with any borrowings, funds maintenance and the acquisition pipeline within the leverage limits.
plainEnglish: The rule that the trust must hand over at least 90% of its spare cash to investors, keeping it back for them rather than sitting on it. It is why these products pay regular income.

definition: The SEBI framework prescribes limits on borrowings and the loan-to-value of assets for REITs and InvITs, with the permissible level described in the regulations and additional conditions when the limit is approached, including unit-holder approvals in specified cases. Leverage amplifies both distributions and losses, so unit holders should monitor the trust's loan-to-value and debt-servicing cover alongside payouts. Refinancing risk rises when a large maturity falls during stressed markets.
plainEnglish: The borrowing cap that keeps these trusts from mortgaging themselves. Some debt is allowed to buy assets faster; too much turns an income product into a gamble.

definition: Term insurance is pure protection cover under which the insurer pays the sum assured to the nominee if the insured dies within the policy term and pays nothing if the insured survives, in exchange for regular premiums. Because there is no maturity benefit or investment component, term premiums are low relative to the cover, making it the efficient way to protect dependants against loss of income. Indian insurers offer level-term, increasing-cover and return-of-premium variants, the last of which is materially costlier for the same protection.
plainEnglish: Life cover with nothing left over at the end: if you die during the term, your family gets the money; if you live, you have paid for peace of mind. The cheapest way to protect a family.

definition: Whole life insurance provides cover for the insured's entire lifetime, with a savings element in participating and non-linked variants through which the policy accumulates value that can be surrendered or borrowed against, subject to conditions. Premiums are payable for a chosen period or for life, and maturity benefits are typically paid at a specified age or on death if earlier. Relative to term insurance, whole life products combine protection and long-duration savings with costs and caps prescribed by IRDAI product regulations.
plainEnglish: Cover that lasts your whole lifetime rather than a fixed number of years, with money building up inside it over time. You pay more than pure term cover for the lifelong promise and the savings pot.

definition: An endowment plan is a traditional with-profits life insurance policy that pays the sum assured plus accrued bonuses on survival to maturity, and the death benefit to the nominee if the insured dies during the term. Premiums are higher than term cover because the policy is both protection and a contractually structured savings product with guaranteed and non-guaranteed elements as prescribed under IRDAI product rules. Its internal rate of return should be evaluated against the investor's alternatives rather than by the absolute maturity amount displayed.
plainEnglish: A bundle: life insurance plus forced savings. Survive to the end and you get a lump sum with bonuses; die early and your family gets the money.

definition: A unit linked insurance plan combines life cover with investment in market-linked funds chosen by the policyholder, with the policy value represented by units whose NAV reflects the performance of the selected fund, subject to a minimum guarantee on the sum assured component. IRDAI's linked-product regulations cap premium allocation charges, fund management charges, policy administration charges and discontinuance charges, and prescribe a lock-in period before surrender or partial withdrawal is permitted. ULIP returns are returns to the underlying fund minus the charges deducted, so charge structures and switching options materially affect outcomes.
plainEnglish: Insurance where your premium is invested in funds like a mutual fund, with a life-cover wrapper. Good if charges are low; disappointing if the fee table is thick.

definition: A money-back policy is a traditional life insurance contract that pays defined survival benefits at intervals during the term and a reduced sum assured, plus bonuses where applicable, on maturity, while the full death benefit applies if the insured dies during the term. It is structurally similar to an endowment with scheduled partial payouts, and its effective return depends on the date pattern of those payouts. Policyholders should compute the internal rate of return of the cash-flow schedule rather than comparing headline totals.
plainEnglish: Insurance that pays you a slice of the maturity amount every few years to spend, with the rest plus bonuses at the end. The money feels free along the way, but the total return is what matters.

definition: The sum assured is the amount the insurer contractually pays on the occurrence of the insured event, typically death, with its computation and any bonuses or additional benefit amounts defined in the policy schedule and filed product terms. In ULIPs, the sum assured must satisfy the minimum multiple of premium or policy value prescribed under IRDAI's linked-product regulations, and for traditional policies it is fixed at underwriting. It is the correct number, not the accumulated premium, against which the adequacy of life cover is assessed.
plainEnglish: The cheque the insurer writes to your family if the worst happens. Check it against your loans, income and future expenses, not against what you paid in.

definition: The mortality charge is the cost of providing life cover, deducted periodically from a ULIP's fund value or built into traditional policy pricing, equal to the insurer's expected death claims adjusted for expenses and margins. In ULIPs it is disclosed in the charge table and is deducted through unit cancellation according to the regulations, making transparent net-of-charge returns the only honest measure of the policy. The charge rises with the insured's age and with the amount at risk under the policy.
plainEnglish: The part of your premium that literally buys the life insurance inside the plan, deducted regularly as you age. The rest is your investment; this is the cost of the cover.

definition: A rider is an add-on benefit attached to a base policy for an additional premium, covering contingencies such as accidental death, disability, critical illness or hospitalisation within the framework permitted by IRDAI's product regulations. Riders extend or supplement the base cover but cannot be purchased standalone and expire when the base policy ends, subject to product terms. Their value depends on the extra premium versus equivalent standalone cover.
plainEnglish: Optional extras bolted onto your policy, like accident cover or critical-illness protection, for a small extra fee. Always compare their price with a standalone policy.

definition: The surrender value is the amount the policyholder receives on terminating a life insurance policy early, measured as a guaranteed surrender value plus, where applicable, a special surrender value for traditional policies after the minimum premium-paying period, and as the fund value less discontinuance charges for ULIPs after the lock-in under IRDAI's linked-product rules. Early surrender typically destroys a significant portion of premiums paid, which is why policies should never be bought without the intention to fund them as intended. The exact formula is prescribed in the policy document for each product.
plainEnglish: The cash-back figure if you quit a policy halfway. Usually far less than you paid, because insurers load their costs into the early years.

definition: The free-look period is a window prescribed by IRDAI after receipt of the policy document during which the policyholder may return the policy for cancellation and receive a refund of premium less the expenses permitted under the regulations. It exists to counter misselling by giving the buyer an unconditional exit immediately after seeing the actual terms. The window runs from the date the document is delivered, and policies sold through distance or electronic channels follow the regulations applicable to that channel.
plainEnglish: A cooling-off window after the policy arrives: read the fine print, and if you have been sold something unsuitable, hand it back for a refund minus a small deduction.

definition: An annuity is a contract under which the policyholder pays a lump sum or series of premiums to an insurer and receives periodic payments for a defined period or lifetime, with variants such as immediate and deferred annuities, life annuities with or without return of purchase price, and joint-life options. Payments can be level, increasing at a prescribed rate, or market-linked through variable annuity products within the framework regulated by IRDAI. In India, annuities are the mandatory income mechanism for a portion of retirement accumulations from products such as NPS and pension plans, and they convert longevity risk into insurer risk.
plainEnglish: Buying yourself a lifelong salary: hand over a lump sum, get fixed monthly payments as long as you live. The insurer carries the risk you live very long.

definition: The National Pension System is a contributory, market-linked retirement savings scheme regulated by PFRDA, open to citizens and to corporate and government sectors, with investments allocated across asset classes including equity, corporate debt, government securities and alternative assets under the investment guidelines and tiers offered by the scheme. Accumulations grow with the chosen asset mix through pension funds and are accessed at superannuation subject to the prescribed conditions, with a mandatory annuitisation of a portion of the corpus upon exit. Additional tax treatment for the scheme and for corporate contributions is provided under the Income-tax Act's specific provisions for the scheme.
plainEnglish: A government-regulated retirement pot where you and possibly your employer pay in regularly, the money is invested in funds you choose, and at retirement part of it buys you a pension.

definition: The Employees' Pension Scheme is the statutory pension component of the retirement framework administered by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, under which a portion of the employer's contribution is diverted to provide monthly member pension based on pensionable salary and pensionable service, subject to the scheme's ceilings and formulas. Pension vests after the minimum qualifying service prescribed in the scheme, with widow, children and disability pension variants provided. Disputes over higher salary pensions and the scheme's actuarial position have been the subject of litigation and reform discussion.
plainEnglish: The pension half of the EPF umbrella: your employer's contribution also buys you a modest monthly income after you retire, calculated from your salary and years of service.

definition: The Public Provident Fund is a long-tenure small-savings scheme with a statutory maturity period, annual contribution limits prescribed by the scheme rules, tax-free interest and tax-deductible contributions within the limits of the scheme and the Income-tax Act, offering partial withdrawal and loan facilities subject to conditions. Interest rates are administratively notified each quarter by the government rather than being market-determined. Its sovereign guarantee and tax treatment make it a benchmark low-risk compounding vehicle for household savings.
plainEnglish: A fifteen-year government savings account: put in an amount every year, earn tax-free interest fixed by the government each quarter, and take a tax deduction on what you put in.

definition: The Atal Pension Yojana is a government-subsidised pension scheme for subscribers in the unorganised sector, administered through banks and post offices and regulated by PFRDA, under which a subscriber contributes periodically until the prescribed age and receives guaranteed minimum monthly pension slabs thereafter, with the option of the spouse continuing the pension and the nominee receiving the corpus in specified cases. The government guarantees the minimum pension and co-contributed for a limited early period of the scheme under the original terms. Eligibility has been revised over time, including income-tax-payee exclusions, and the current conditions should be checked with an updated scheme notification.
plainEnglish: A small monthly pension for workers without formal retirement plans: pay small amounts while you work, and the government tops up so you get at least a guaranteed pension slab for life.

definition: The Liberalised Remittance Scheme permits resident individuals, including minors through guardians, to remit funds abroad up to the prescribed annual limit for permitted current and capital account transactions, such as education, travel, gifts, investment in securities and property, under the RBI's framework. Remittances are routed through authorised dealer banks, and certain transactions are prohibited or require conditions, and tax collected at source applies on specified remittances at rates prescribed by the Income-tax Act and Finance Acts. Breaching the limit or the purpose categories has consequences under FEMA.
plainEnglish: The annual allowance for sending money abroad legally as an individual, for investing, studying or travelling. The bank processes it, the tax department may collect some advance tax on it, and the cap resets each year.

definition: FEMA is the statute governing India's foreign-exchange regime, classifying transactions into current-account and capital-account categories, establishing that India maintains a current-account convertibility regime and regulating capital flows through rules, notifications and the RBI's directions. It replaced the older FERA framework with a pro-management rather than criminal-first philosophy for ordinary violations, while retaining penalties and enforcement powers. Practically all foreign remittances, cross-border investment and overseas asset holdings by residents derive their legal framework from FEMA and the rules made under it.
plainEnglish: The law that decides what Indians can legally do with foreign money, from sending it abroad to holding shares overseas. Current transactions like travel and education are easy, capital moves come with conditions.

definition: An American depositary receipt is a negotiable certificate issued by a depositary bank in the United States representing shares of a non-US company, allowing US investors to trade the foreign stock in dollars and during US market hours. Indian ADRs, such as those historically listed by major IT and banking companies, trade on US exchanges subject to US securities regulation and the company's level of registration and reporting. The ADR price reflects the underlying Indian share price converted through the rupee exchange rate, adjusting for the receipt ratio and any premium or discount in the two markets.
plainEnglish: A receipt that lets Americans buy Indian company shares on New York exchanges in dollars. Underneath, it is still the same company and the same shares.

definition: A global depositary receipt is a depositary certificate for shares of a company, typically issued and traded outside its home country, with Indian GDRs historically listed on European exchanges such as Luxembourg and London, allowing Indian issuers to raise capital abroad. The instrument represents underlying equity shares held by the depositary, with rights and conversion mechanics disclosed in the offering documents and subject to the FEMA framework governing issuance. Investors should distinguish genuine GDR programs from structures that were used to circumvent capital controls, which led to regulatory tightening and safeguards.
plainEnglish: A certificate for Indian shares traded on international exchanges, mostly in Europe, letting foreign investors hold the stock without trading in India directly.

definition: An Indian depositary receipt is a security issued by a depositary representing shares of a foreign company, listed and traded on Indian exchanges and denominated in rupees, under the framework prescribed by SEBI. It allows an overseas issuer to access Indian investors without a direct listing, but IDR issuance has been rare in practice and the segment has seen minimal activity. Key terms such as conversion ratio, voting conventions and fungibility with the home-market shares are set out in the issue documents.
plainEnglish: The mirror image of an ADR: a receipt letting Indian investors buy a foreign company's shares on Indian exchanges, in rupees. Allowed by the rules, but hardly ever used.

fullName: Overseas Fund of Fund or International Scheme
definition: An international mutual fund is an Indian mutual fund scheme that invests in overseas securities, either directly under the category permitted by SEBI's categorisation framework or indirectly by investing in units of an overseas fund, giving rupee-based investors exposure to foreign markets without using their own remittance allowance. Such schemes carry currency risk in addition to market risk, and the overall overseas investment limits applicable to the industry and per scheme are prescribed by the regulatory framework and can constrain fresh subscriptions at times. Their performance includes the effect of rupee appreciation or depreciation that resident investors do not control.
plainEnglish: A local fund that buys foreign shares for you, so your returns reflect both how those markets perform and how the rupee moves against the dollar.

definition: A foreign portfolio investor is a non-resident entity registered with SEBI through a designated depository participant to invest in Indian securities, subject to categories, eligibility conditions, position limits and disclosure norms designed to distinguish genuine portfolio flows from control-oriented investment. FPIs include foreign institutional investors, funds, and sovereign and other eligible entities, and they route investments through Indian custody and settlement infrastructure. FPI flows are a significant driver of domestic market liquidity, and aggregate ownership limits are set to leave control of Indian companies in resident hands.
plainEnglish: A licensed foreign investor in Indian shares and bonds, regulated like a guest at the table: free to buy and sell within limits, registered and disclosed.

definition: Foreign direct investment is investment by a non-resident in the capital of an Indian entity through equity or instruments convertible into equity with a lasting interest in management, permitted under the automatic route or requiring government approval depending on the sector. Sectoral caps and conditions, including those on downstream investments and investment from land-border countries, are prescribed in the foreign-exchange rules, the consolidated FDI policy and sectoral regulations. FDI is distinct from foreign portfolio investment because it seeks control or lasting interest rather than trading positions.
plainEnglish: Foreign money buying a real stake in an Indian business, usually with a say in how it runs. Some industries welcome it automatically; others need government clearance.

definition: A currency hedged fund uses forward contracts or similar instruments to neutralise the effect of rupee-dollar or other exchange-rate movements on the returns of its overseas exposure, so the investor receives the underlying asset's return without the translation swing. Hedging costs depend on interest-rate differentials between the currencies and are embedded in forward pricing, reducing the fund's return relative to the unhedged version when the rupee is expected to weaken. The choice between hedged and unhedged exposure is therefore a view on the underlying asset and on currency competitiveness together.
plainEnglish: A foreign investment with the currency wobble switched off, so you get the market's return in dollar terms converted without rupee surprises. The insurance costs a little.

definition: Currency risk is the potential for adverse exchange-rate movements to reduce the rupee value of an overseas investment or to alter the competitiveness of cross-border cash flows, and it operates independently of the underlying asset's own performance. An Indian investor in US equities earns the asset return plus the dollar-rupee move, either of which can dominate over short horizons. Hedging, diversification across currency exposure and simple acceptance of the risk are the available responses.
plainEnglish: The risk that the rupee does something to your foreign money. A US stock can rise in dollars while your rupee return falls if the rupee strengthens.

definition: Private equity is the asset class of equity investments in unlisted companies or in listed companies taken private, spanning venture capital, growth capital, buyouts and special situations, typically through pooled funds with long lock-ins and low liquidity. Indian private equity operates under the SEBI AIF framework for pooled vehicles and is a principal source of growth capital for unlisted enterprises, with exits through IPOs, strategic sales or secondary transfers. Returns are highly dispersed across managers, making manager selection and vintage diversification more important than average asset-class statistics.
plainEnglish: Money that buys ownership in businesses that are not on the stock exchange, holds them for years, improves or grows them, and sells later. Patient capital with big wins and big write-offs.

definition: Venture capital is a subset of private equity focused on early-stage companies with high growth potential and high failure rates, generally investing after angel or seed rounds and before growth-stage private equity, with capital deployed in tranches against milestones. Indian venture capital operates through AIF Category I vehicles among others and is central to the country's start-up financing ecosystem, with exits primarily via later rounds, acquisitions or listings. The power-law return distribution of venture portfolios means a minority of investments produce most of the gains.
plainEnglish: Funding for young, risky start-ups that banks will not touch. Most bets fail, a few rocket, and that is the point of the maths.

definition: An alternative investment fund is a privately pooled investment vehicle registered with SEBI that collects funds from sophisticated investors for investment under defined strategies, governed by the AIF Regulations which classify vehicles into three categories with differing permissible strategies, leverage rules and investor bases. AIFs may not solicit the public, have minimum investment thresholds and investor-count limits prescribed by the regulations, and are a key structure for venture capital, private equity, private credit and hedge-fund strategies in India. Category I funds focused on start-ups, SMEs, infrastructure and social impact enjoy specified regulatory concessions.
plainEnglish: A regulated private club for big investors: the vehicle through which professionals pool money for strategies that mutual funds are not allowed to run.

definition: Category I alternative investment funds invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, SMEs, infrastructure, social enterprises or other sectors or areas that the government or regulators consider economically or socially desirable, receiving specified regulatory and tax concessions. The category covers venture capital funds, SME funds, social impact funds, infrastructure funds and the newer special-situation variants within the framework. Leverage is restricted, and the funds invest primarily in unlisted securities as permitted for each sub-category.
plainEnglish: The most encouraged flavour of private fund: the ones that back start-ups, small businesses, infrastructure and social projects. The rules treat them kindly.

definition: Category II alternative investment funds are privately pooled vehicles that neither fall under Category I nor employ the leverage and complex strategies of Category III, covering private equity funds, debt funds and funds for distressed assets within the AIF framework.
